At three-month follow-up, the patient reported pain rated 4/10 occurring several times per week and subsequently underwent total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplantation for definitive management.ConclusionThis case describes an association between OMT and short-term pain improvement within a multimodal treatment strategy for chronic pancreatitis-related visceral pain. Although causality cannot be established from a single uncontrolled observation, the findings support further investigation of OMT as a potential adjunctive therapy in pediatric patients with chronic pancreatitis and secondary visceral hyperalgesia.

items.title: Explainable machine learning for preoperative prediction of acute kidney injury after intertrochanteric fracture surgery in older adults
items.abstract: BackgroundAcute kidney injury (AKI) is an important postoperative complication in older patients undergoing surgery for intertrochanteric femoral fracture. This study aimed to develop and internally evaluate an explainable model for preoperative AKI risk assessment.MethodsThis retrospective study included 616 patients aged ≥60 years, including 54 (8.8%) who developed postoperative AKI. Candidate predictors were processed and selected using development-cohort data, and seven machine-learning algorithms were compared. Model performance was assessed across 100 repeated stratified 70/30 partitions and by 500-repetition model-specific and complete-pipeline bootstrap analyses. Calibration, decision-curve analysis, and SHAP were used to evaluate and interpret the selected model.ResultsThe reported Naive Bayes model comprised baseline serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, chloride, uric acid, and chronic kidney disease or renal insufficiency. Across 100 repeated partitions, its mean validation AUC was 0.7231 (SD, 0.0260). The optimism-corrected AUC was 0.8004 for the fixed five-predictor Naive Bayes specification and 0.756 when the complete development pipeline was repeated; the latter analysis yielded a corrected Brier score of 0.084, calibration intercept of 0.02, and calibration slope of 1.70. In the original algorithm-comparison cohort, the observed AUC was 0.795 (95% CI, 0.698–0.892). When the first serum creatinine measurement obtained after admission was used as the alternative reference value, the number of AKI events decreased from 54 to 43 and the validation AUC was 0.706 (95% CI, 0.586–0.826).ConclusionThe model showed moderate internal discrimination across repeated partitions. Model-specific and complete-pipeline bootstrap analyses provided complementary estimates of internal optimism. The model may complement routine preoperative renal assessment while its calibration and transportability are evaluated in additional cohorts.

items.title: Clinical challenges in vaccine and monoclonal antibody development against ESCAPE pathogens: insights from EMA scientific advice procedures
items.abstract: BackgroundCombating ESCAPE pathogens (E. faecium, S. aureus, C. difficile, A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa, and Enterobacteriaceae) remains a major public health concern due to their treatment resistance and immune evasion. Vaccines and monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) are promising solutions, yet only one mAb is licensed and no vaccine has reached that stage. To identify recurring clinical challenges, we analyzed final advice letters (FALs) issued through the European Medicines Agency's (EMA) Scientific Advice procedure.MethodsWe searched both the Paul-Ehrlich-Institut local database and the EMA database for FALs on vaccines and mAbs targeting ESCAPE pathogens. We included FALs that matched the pathogen and product criteria and addressed clinical development. We excluded those focused solely on quality, non-clinical, safety, or post-marketing aspects. From the included FALs, we extracted information across four main categories: primary endpoint, statistical analyses, study population, and study design. Regulatory responses were classified as fully, silently, partially, or not endorsed. We subsequently reviewed related clinical trial protocols to assess whether recommendations were implemented and to provide a narrative summary of changes to the development programs.ResultsWe included 14 FALs for each of the two medicine categories, related to six vaccine and 13 mAb trials. To address common challenges across the primary endpoints, regulators recommended selecting single, infection-related endpoints and emphasized precise clinical and laboratory case definitions to ensure attribution of infection to the target pathogen. They further advised on incorporating supportive evidence, such as subgroup analyses of cases or inflammation markers, direct microbiological or indirect measures (e.g., antibiotic use, hospital stay), or survival-related endpoints. Recommendations for study populations focused on refining the inclusion/exclusion criteria to identify those most likely to benefit. Regulators also advised on changes in the statistical analysis plan (mainly due to lower-than-expected incidence) and generally discouraged single pivotal trials.ConclusionThe development of vaccines and mAbs against ESCAPE pathogens is challenged by pathogen diversity, unpredictable infection rates, heterogeneous trial populations, and diagnostic uncertainty. In a field with no one-size-fits-all development pathway, early regulatory interaction and multidisciplinary disease-expert input are essential to reduce uncertainty and support robust, efficient clinical development programs.

items.title: Extensive vulvar and perianal langerhans cell histiocytosis with clinical improvement during low-dose thalidomide and topical therapy: a case report
items.abstract: Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) involving the female genital region is uncommon and can closely resemble chronic inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic vulvar diseases. We report a case of a 35-year-old woman with a 6-month history of recurrent painful brownish-red plaques, nodules, erosions, and ulcerations that began in the perianal region and subsequently extended to the vulva. Topical fusidic acid only provided temporary symptomatic relief. Histopathological examination revealed epidermal erosion and crusting, acanthosis, elongated rete ridges, and a dense dermal and subcutaneous infiltrate containing numerous large histiocytes with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and focal nuclear grooves. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed that the lesional cells exhibited positivity for S100, CD1a, and langerin and negative for HMB45, SOX10, ALK-1A4, and BRAF V600E. Broader molecular testing for MAPK-pathway alterations was not performed, and the lesion was therefore described as BRAF V600E-immunonegative rather than genetically BRAF/MAPK wild type. The pathological diagnosis was vulvar LCH, with clinically suspected involvement of the perianal region. Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) revealed an enlarged cervical lymph node, with no other abnormalities documented; its relationship to LCH could not be determined. Oral thalidomide (50 mg nightly) was subsequently administered while topical Pevisone was continued. Symptomatic improvement, particularly pain relief, was observed after 1 week, and further clinical improvement of the anogenital lesions was documented at 3 months. Because both therapies were used concomitantly, the independent contribution of thalidomide could not be determined. This case underscores the diagnostic challenges associated with anogenital LCH and documents short-term clinical improvement during a low-dose thalidomide-containing regimen without establishing thalidomide monotherapy efficacy. It also highlights the necessity for biopsy, comprehensive systemic evaluation, and ongoing follow-up.

items.title: Bovine H5N1 influenza viruses have adapted to more efficiently use receptors abundant in cattle
items.abstract: Sustained mammal-to-mammal transmission of high pathogenicity H5N1 avian influenza viruses is reshaping the host range of these pathogens. One of the longest-running mammalian transmission chains involves the B3.13 genotype circulating in U.S. dairy cattle which was detected in early 2024. Genomic analyses revealed selection and rapid fixation of haemagglutinin mutations D104G and V147M. We demonstrate, via glycomic profiling, that bovine tissues, including the mammary gland, are enriched in N- and O-linked glycans capped with N-glycolylneuraminic acid (NeuGc), a sialic acid which is not synthesised by humans and birds, which instead express only N-acetylneuraminic acid (NeuAc). Early cattle H5 viruses poorly recognised NeuGc, but D104G and V147M enabled efficient engagement of both NeuAc- and NeuGc-containing receptors. These mutations enhanced replication in bovine mammary tissue without major attenuation of replication in human lung and primary nasal epithelial cells. NeuGc-driven receptor adaptation therefore promotes viral fitness in cattle without majorly changing zoonotic risk. Deep mutational scanning was able to identify alternative haemagglutinin substitutions that confer NeuGc usage and represent surveillance markers for emerging cattle H5 lineages. Finally, structural analyses suggest a potential molecular mechanism for the dual binding of the cattle-adapted viruses.
items.authors: Hassard, J. A.; Yang, J.; Hawkins, D. E. D. P.; Pekar, J. E.; Dadonaite, B.; Yu, J.; Richardson, S. A. S.; Pinto, R. M.; Ramirez Valdez, K.; Lemey, P.; Quantrill, J. M.; Peacock, T. P.

items.title: Inflammation-driven cellular selection impacts X-linked mosaicism in the epidermis
items.abstract: In eutherian females, the choice of which X chromosome gets embryonically inactivated is thought to be random. Somatic tissues are thus assumed to comprise cells with a 50:50 ratio of maternal:paternal X active. However, a phenomenon known as X-skewing has been observed, wherein tissue composition shifts to be dominated by cells expressing one X or the other. On a gross level, such X-skewing is phenotypically silent except in the case where one X-chromosome carries a disease mutation. Here, by leveraging a mouse model of an X-linked disease called Incontinentia Pigmenti, caused by heterozygous mutations in the NF-kB effector, Nemo, we explore how X-linked cellular dynamics shape progenitor biology in the epidermis. Lineage tracing with X-linked reporters shows that at birth, the epidermis is unexpectedly skewed toward mutant cells. Within a week, as inflammation emerges, these dynamics reverse leaving surviving animals with almost entirely wild-type epithelium. The shift is driven by loss rather than growth since mutant cells adopt an aberrant fate and die at higher rates than their wild-type neighbours; proliferation rises in both populations. Notably, wild-type proliferation scales with local tissue composition, suggesting these cells calibrate their response to the extent of the mutant burden to compensate appropriately for tissue loss. Depleting macrophages, the principal TNF- source, attenuates inflammation, mutant cell death and ultimately is expected to preserve the mutant population. Altogether, our results identify inflammation as a selective force capable of resolving deleterious mosaicism, not only in the context of an X-linked disease, but within any dynamic, clonally heterogeneous epithelium.
items.authors: Angelopoulou, E.; Gandhi, K.; van Wolfswinkel, M.; Schmautz, L.; Oyarzun, I.; Nowosadtko, S.; Fischer, I.; Schwartz, V.; Griss, J. J.; Ellis, S. J.

items.title: Contrasting relationships between evolved consumer diversity and productivity for essential vs. substitutable resources
items.abstract: Any mechanistic biodiversity-ecosystem functioning theory must explain how biodiversity in natural communities arises, which requires an evolutionary metacommunity perspective. Using a model of adaptive evolution of competitive metacommunities in landscapes with spatially heterogeneous supply of two resources, we studied the evolution of resource-uptake specialization as a function of resource type (substitutable/essential) and trade-off shape between resource-uptake affinities (generalist-/specialist-favouring). We identified "critical essentiality" as a key phenomenon separating parameter regions with fundamentally different biodiversity--ecosystem function relationships. Specifically, while greater spatial heterogeneity in resource supply increases biodiversity, this comes at the cost of reduced productivity when resources are essential. Moreover, when resources are essential, both generalist- and specialist-favoring trade-offs select for phenotypes that prevent efficient resource partitioning, leading to low resource use efficiency and consumer biomass - despite often high species richness. In contrast, when resources are substitutable, a specialist-favoring affinity trade-off selects for phenotypes that partition resources efficiently, promoting a metacommunity of only two species characterized by high functional diversity, resource use efficiency, and biomass. Overall, our analyses thus suggest that conditions promoting the evolution of diverse consumer communities often do not engender higher functional richness, consumer biomass, or resource use efficiency.
items.authors: Gopakumar, A.; Diehl, S.; Brännström, A.

items.title: WildObserve: Camera-trap image review software that learns species labels during annotation
items.abstract: Motion-activated camera traps are an effective tool for monitoring animals, but a single study can produce millions of images, which must be analyzed before they yield data. The burden of analyzing them has led many teams to automate the work with computer vision. These models lose accuracy on images unlike those they were trained on, however, and a general model may not use the categories a project needs. Adapting a model to a project usually requires at least one of the following: many labeled images per species, programming expertise, a graphics processing unit (GPU), or uploading images to a remote server. I describe WildObserve, a desktop application that adapts to each project without any of these requirements. Before a reviewer sees an image, MegaDetector finds animals, people, and vehicles and marks images that are likely empty, and SpeciesNet suggests a species for each animal. WildObserve keeps SpeciesNet's feature vector for each animal, so as the reviewer confirms or corrects labels, a project model (a logistic regression on those features) retrains in about a second on an ordinary laptop, learning the project's own species list and names. Images stay on the user's computer, model outputs and human decisions are kept separate, and exports record review and model provenance. On the Caltech Camera Traps dataset, WildObserve processed 8.1 images/s on an Apple M1 Pro laptop with Core ML (1.5 images/s on its CPU), species suggestions included. At a 0.5 threshold, it found animals in 97.1% of animal images but also put a box on 48.0% of images labeled empty. On 1,467 animal crops from 14 categories, SpeciesNet alone reached 0.919 balanced accuracy. The project model reached 0.886 with three labels per category and 0.937 with 25, and 0.931 on camera locations absent from its training labels; built on features from DINOv2, a general-purpose image model, it reached only 0.784 with 50. On the Oregon Critters dataset, released after SpeciesNet was trained, SpeciesNet reached 0.751 and the project model passed it with only ten labels per category (0.783). WildObserve gives a project species suggestions in its own categories, from a model it trains simply by reviewing, without writing code, needing a GPU, or sending images elsewhere.
items.authors: Tabak, M.

items.title: Rapid trait adaptation has contrasting effects on different dimensions of stability under environmental change
items.abstract: Environmental change alters species growth rates and, through species interactions, can produce complex effects on community functioning and composition. Because functional traits mediate both environmental responses and competition, rapid trait adaptation may modify these effects, but its consequences in multispecies communities remain unclear. We used a trait-based model of competitive communities to test how adaptation affects the mean and diversity of species growth responses to environmental change, and how this influences functional and compositional resistance (how unaffected the community is by the environmental change) and resilience (how well it recovers after it has acclimated to the altered environment). Adaptation altered response variance more strongly than the mean by changing the balance between environmental optimisation and competition-driven trait divergence. As a result, adaptation strongly increased compositional stability, but had less clear effects on abundance. Adaptation also generated a trade-off between resistance and resilience: faster adaptation improved resistance but reduced resilience as communities were displaced less by the environmental change and thus recovered less. Overall, adaptation can be stabilising, but higher adaptation rates do not necessarily produce greater stability across all stability components.
items.authors: Holmes, M.; Yamamichi, M.; De Laender, F.

items.title: Compatible Comma-Free Codes and the Origin of the Genetic Code
items.abstract: The genetic code is the rule that (apart from minor modifications) is used by all contemporary life on Earth to translate genes into proteins. It is summarized by a 4x4x4 table which maps the 64 possible triplet RNA codons to the 20 canonical amino acids ("AAs"). Understanding the origin of this code is a fundamental open problem in biology. We review the idea of a comma-free code, and put forward a general reason to suspect the primordial code was comma-free (even though the modern code is not). We explain why this primordial code should then persist as a comma-free subcode within the modern code, and identify the five optimal candidates for such a subcode. We then introduce the idea of "compatible comma-free codes" and explain how they allow multiple codes to evolve in parallel, circumventing a standard argument suggesting that code evolution should effectively freeze when the associated genome becomes sufficiently complex. In particular, we highlight the possibility that the original code was a comma-free doublet code, which was then overtaken by a compatible comma-free triplet code, which finally evolved (after the evolution of the start codon and ribosome) to the modern saturated triplet code. To assess this idea, we classify all inequivalent compatible comma-free doublet-triplet codes and, among these, identify the three most promising predecessors of the modern code. Consistency between these three best codes and the "wobble rules" in gene translation provide non-trivial evidence for this possibility.
items.authors: Boyle, L.; Boyle, L.

items.title: Organelle intergenic DNA is preferentially distributed between opposite-polarity gene pairs.
items.abstract: Across eukaryotes, mitochondrial and plastid genomes vary enormously in size and noncoding content. This variation is often attributed to diverging mutation rates, DNA repair mechanisms, and the power of genetic drift. Although these processes can help explain how much noncoding DNA an organelle genome may retain, they do not explain how this noncoding DNA is distributed throughout the genome. We analyzed over 2.6 million intergenic regions (IGRs) from ~37,000 mitochondrial and plastid genomes to test whether gene-pair polarity marks local differences in the distribution of organelle intergenic DNA. Taxonomy-structured mixed models, controlling for flanking-gene length and type, showed that IGRs between opposite-polarity gene pairs were 1.1-3.2-fold longer than those between same-polarity genes. IGRs between convergent (+-) and divergent (-+) gene pairs showed distinct residual-dispersion patterns, indicating that they are not homogeneous in their length distribution. The prevalence of opposite-polarity gene pairs showed no consistent relationship with organelle genome size or intergenic DNA fraction. Ultimately then, gene-pair polarity consistently marks where organelle intergenic DNA is preferentially located.
items.authors: Sanita Lima, M.; Dupin, B.; Smith, D. R.

items.title: Additive in size, synergistic in composition: selection across the eastern oyster larval genome under coastal acidification and sewage effluent
items.abstract: Coastal organisms experience natural and anthropogenic stressors simultaneously, yet the interactive effects of multiple stressors are largely unknown. In urbanized estuaries, coastal acidification (CA) is coupled to sewage effluent (SE): nutrient loading from SE stimulates microbial CO2 production, and this lowers the pH. The genomic targets of selection of CA and SE have been characterized separately but never together in early life stages of marine organisms. Here, we exposed eastern oyster (Crassostrea virginica) larvae to control, CA (~2800 atm pCO2), SE (5% by volume), and the combination (CASE) for 24 h across independent spawns, and used expressed exome capture sequencing to measure allele-frequency change before and after exposure, removing loci that also shifted in controls. CASE generally produced the lowest survival, although mortality was driven primarily by effluent and did not exceed the additive expectation. The size of allele-frequency change under CASE stayed close to the additive sum of the single stressors, but it showed compositional synergy: CASE had more outlier loci than CA and SE combined with 1,941 loci (747 genes) detected only under the combined treatment. CASE outliers were enriched for proteostasis, ciliary function, mitochondrial calcium handling, and a steroid-metabolizing (CYP17) module consistent with effluent endocrine disruptors. Selection acted repeatedly on standing variation across spawns and genetic backgrounds, with the largest allele-frequency shifts at rare, spawn-private loci. Enriched biological functions recurred across spawns more often than expected, while most outlier loci were specific to one or two spawns, consistent with genotypic redundancy. Our results show that combined stressors can recruit a compositionally synergistic genomic response, at loci and functions not detected under either stressor alone, even when survival and the size of allele-frequency change are additive.
items.authors: Puritz, J. B.; Harvey, J. A.; Lotterhos, K.

items.title: Phylogenetic evidence for the emergence of bacterial σ-factors by domain fusion
items.abstract: {sigma}-factors are dissociable subunits of RNA polymerase (RNAP), forming the basal regulatory machinery for bacterial transcription. The minimal {sigma}-factors contain two domains (called {sigma}2 or {sigma}4), both of which bind RNAP as well as the promoter DNA through their helix-turn-helix motif. Housekeeping {sigma}-factors contain four domains. We identify proteins containing at least one of the four {sigma}-factor domains in bacterial and bacteriophage genomes; we also show that proteins containing either {sigma}2 or {sigma}4, which are not defined as {sigma}-factors, are commonly found in both sets of organisms. Using phylogenetic analysis of these two domains, we suggest that the highly conserved major housekeeping {sigma}-factor, with its complex domain architecture, represents a late-evolving monophyletic clade, whereas single-domain proteins and minimal {sigma}-factor architectures comprising {sigma}2 and {sigma}4 might be ancestral. Thus, {sigma}-factors probably evolved from single-domain DNA-binding transcription factors by domain accretion.
items.authors: Tiwary, P.; Seshasayee, A. S. N.

items.title: Gene-level evolutionary conservation and human constraint decline at comparable rates across the age of onset of Mendelian disease
items.abstract: Background Gene-level constraint and conservation scores are widely used to prioritise disease genes and to benchmark genomic language models. Purifying selection acts weakly on phenotypes manifesting after reproduction, so these scores are expected to carry less information about late-onset disease. An onset-dependent gradient has been demonstrated for human allele frequencies but not for the gene-level scores used in practice. Results We built an age-of-onset axis for 2,885 Mendelian diseases from Orphanet and fitted cross-species conservation (241-way phyloP) and human-population constraint (shet) on the same 5,322 gene-disease pairs against matched controls, to test whether one decays faster with onset. Their onset slopes differed by 0.23 logit units (97.5% confidence interval -0.10 to 0.56), equivalent to 0.024 units of area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) in a design resolving 0.049; the interval excludes constraint losing discriminative power faster than conservation by more than 0.011 AUROC units, widening to 0.033 when somatic associations are dropped. The usual explanation, that early-onset disease genes are developmental, pleiotropic and haploinsufficient by construction, did not account for the contrast; conditioning barely moved it. The answer did, however, depend on the constraint metric: three alternatives yielded larger contrasts excluding zero, though paired comparison could not distinguish the estimates. The metrics also diverged on recessive disease genes, with shet ranked below the gene pool (AUROC 0.487) and loss-of-function depletion above it (0.533), though, against matched controls, both ranked them below (0.457 and 0.450). Evolutionary scores improved a non-evolutionary baseline by 17 to 23%, with no onset gradient. Conclusions Conservation and constraint do not lose their value at measurably different rates as disease onset rises, and with only 283 late-onset Mendelian diseases annotated genome-wide, the question cannot be settled more finely. The gene-class explanation does not account for the contrast. Metrics that rank genes near-identically can still yield opposite onset-stratified answers, so a result reported by one metric carries a sensitivity that its confidence interval does not show. No constraint metric identifies recessive disease genes against matched controls, so a pipeline with recessive disease in scope needs a correction that switching metric does not supply.
items.authors: Mahaboob Ali, A. A.; Nelson, E. J. R.

items.title: A chromosome-level genome assembly of the chilli thrips Scirtothrips dorsalis Hood (Thysanoptera: Thripidae)
items.abstract: Thrips are known for being pests of many agricultural crops, as well as vectors of plant viruses. Yet despite their economic importance, genomic resources for this group remain limited, and no chromosome-level genome has been available for the genus Scirtothrips. One such species is the chilli thrips, Scirtothrips dorsalis Hood (Thysanoptera: Thripidae). This invasive and highly polyphagous pest is established across much of the world and transmits several tospoviruses. Genomic resources would provide a new means to understand the traits that make thrips difficult to manage. Here, we present a chromosome-level genome assembly for S. dorsalis. The assembly is 266.5 Mb, with 96.9% of the sequence anchored in 16 chromosome-scale scaffolds. It contains 20,557 genes, and repetitive elements account for 28.8% of the sequence, which is comparable to those of other sequenced Thripidae. A species tree based on 3,019 single copy orthologs placed S. dorsalis as sister to Scirtothrips hansoni, with Scirtothrips most closely related to Frankliniella, Megalurothrips, and Odontothrips. The mitochondrial genome is a single circular molecule of 15,207 bp in which the sequence of the published mini circle is integrated, in contrast to the bipartite mitogenome previously reported for the same cryptic species.
items.authors: Busuulwa, A.; Liesenfelt, T.; Mongue, A. J.; Lahiri, S.

items.title: Sex differences in human musicality are negligible
items.abstract: Since Darwin, researchers have proposed that human musicality evolved in a reproductive context in which males produce music to signal their mate quality to females. Sexually selected traits result from sex differences in the costs of high-quality signal production and high-fidelity signal detection, leading to observable sexual dimorphisms across many species. If musicality is a sexually selected trait in humans, males and females should then differ in their music perception ability, music production ability, or both. The evidence for this possibility is unclear, because previous reports of sex differences in human auditory perception are restricted in scope and inconsistent in direction. Here, we report a test of music processing ability in > 890,000 participants from 208 countries, over a main study and three replication studies. In contrast to other non-musical human traits, and in contrast to music-related traits in non-human animals, we found no consistent advantage in music perception or self-reported music production abilities for either sex. The sex differences we did observe in the main study (n = 554,300) were negligible (Cohen's d range: 0.009-0.111), and Bayesian analyses of general music perception ability indicated evidence in favor of the null hypothesis of no sex difference (Bayes Factor = 0.6). This pattern of results held over the three replication studies. These results imply that the minds of men and women are largely similar when it comes to musicality, and so it is unlikely that sexual selection played any major role in the evolution of human musicality.
items.authors: Bertolo, M.; Müllensiefen, D.; Peretz, I.; Woolley, S. C.; Sakata, J.; Mehr, S.

items.title: Protein Language Model-Conditioned Graph Neural Networks for Multitask Ligand Activity Prediction Across Human GPCRs
items.abstract: Predicting ligand activity across G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) requires models that capture both molecular structure and receptor-specific information while remaining robust to chemical and target-domain shifts. We developed a multimodal graph neural network that combines explicit ligand molecular graphs with frozen protein language model representations of GPCR sequences and jointly predicts quantitative pActivity and binary activity. The model was trained on 271,739 curated ligand-GPCR pairs spanning 183,694 ligands and 216 human GPCRs and evaluated using random, Bemis-Murcko scaffold, and strict cold-ligand partitions. With ESM-2 650M receptor embeddings, the selected model achieved mean absolute errors of 0.513 {+/-} 0.006, 0.540 {+/-} 0.006, and 0.641 {+/-} 0.005 pActivity units under random, cold-ligand, and scaffold evaluation, respectively, substantially outperforming a protein-aware fixed-feature multilayer perceptron and consistently improving quantitative prediction over a matched GINE reference. Removing receptor embeddings markedly degraded both regression and classification, whereas differences among ESM-2 35M, ESM-2 650M, and ProtT5 were comparatively small. Independent evaluation on 6,319 ChEMBL 37/BindingDB pairs revealed a substantial external domain shift, with mean absolute error increasing to approximately 0.94-0.95 despite chemically stringent internal validation. Nevertheless, receptor-specific information remained highly informative in a DRD2-DRD3 selectivity analysis: the cold-ligand ensemble achieved R^2 = 0.853, Spearman {rho} = 0.916, and ROC-AUC = 0.966 for strong DRD3 selectivity, whereas the receptor-independent ablation approached chance-level discrimination. These results establish protein-language-model-conditioned molecular graph learning as a scalable strategy for GPCR bioactivity prediction while identifying chemotype novelty, external-domain transfer, and richer ligand-receptor interaction representations as key remaining challenges.
items.authors: De, M.; Lodh, E.; Majumder, S.; Chowdhury, T.

items.title: PRMT5 inhibition induces a histone methylation switch that drives chromatin plasticity, drug resistance, and metastatic progression
items.abstract: PRMT5 is the major type II protein arginine methyltransferase, regulating fundamental processes including transcription, splicing, and translation. Its expression is restricted to stem and progenitor cells but reactivated in many tumors. Numerous PRMT5 inhibitors (PRMT5i) have been developed, and several are currently in clinical trials. Their efficacy is largely attributed to disruption of PRMT5's role in splicing. Here we show that PRMT5i produce dichotomous effects in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD): they induce lethal splicing defects but also trigger epigenetic changes that actively enable acquisition of drug resistance. Of concern, the resulting stably resistant populations have undergone accelerated dedifferentiation, gaining molecular and phenotypic hallmarks of metastatic disease. Moreover, even brief PRMT5i treatment of drug-naive tumors is sufficient to drive disease progression in vivo. This epigenetic rewiring reflects a previously unappreciated dominance of PRMT5 over PRMT1, arising from differential subcellular localization. Our data indicate that cytoplasmic PRMT5 likely dimethylates histones symmetrically before nuclear import. PRMT5i block this, allowing unmodified histones to reach nuclear PRMT1 and undergo asymmetric dimethylation instead. This symmetric-to-asymmetric switch flips histones from repressive to activating states, yielding rapid chromatin opening and derepression of lineage programs, a subset of which are selected for and retained in resistant cells. Accordingly, inhibition of asymmetric dimethylation suppresses PRMT5i-induced chromatin derepression and synergizes strongly with PRMT5 inhibition. Finally, endogenous PRMT5 suppression in MTAP-deficient human cells partially engages this switch, and CDKN2A/MTAP-deficient tumors are correspondingly more dedifferentiated. Thus, PRMT5i create a splicing vulnerability while simultaneously licensing epigenetic escape toward a more dedifferentiated and aggressive cell state.
items.authors: Fowler, C. E.; O'Hearn, N.; Henning, N.; Griffen, A.; Ye, Z.; Mathey-Andrews, N.; Salus, G.; Hazan, R.; Jacks, T.; Burds, A.; Mueller, H.; Soto-Feliciano, Y.; LaFave, L.; Lees, J.

items.title: Morphogenomic description of Cranifera cranifera (Chitwood, 1932) Kloss, 1960 from captive Blaptica dubia Serville, 1838 cockroach
items.abstract: Nematodes of the superfamily Thelastomatoidea are found in the digestive system of various arthropods, feeding on their host microbiome. They are sometimes considered to be ecologically intermediate forms between free-living rhabditids and parasitic Spirurina, while phylogenetically they are nested within the latter. In addition to new morphological data on the male morphology, this manuscript presents the first nuclear genome assembly of a thelastomatid species, Cranifera cranifera, using long-read sequencing approach, making a total of three nuclear genomes available for superfamilyThelastomatoidea. The C. cranifera nuclear genome assembly presented here is 246 Mb long, consists of 7563 contigs, has an N50 of 43 kb and includes 94% of the BUSCO nematoda_odb12 genes. The mitochondrial genome is 24646 bases long, includes a complete set of protein coding, rRNA and tRNA genes, and a repetitive region 9731 bases long, which includes multiple copies of tRNA-Asn(gtt) and tRNA-Lys(ttt). The nuclear assembly also contained two sequence variants of the 28S rRNA and two of the 18S rRNA genes, highlighting the presence of intragenomic variation within rRNA operon. The newly generated assemblies (nuclear and organelle) will add to a growing body of genomic resources for underrepresented and understudied animal parasitic nematodes from the Clade 3, enabling comprehensive studies in their phylogeny and trait evolution in the future.
items.authors: Morffe, J.; Guiglielmoni, N.; Wassey, N.; Gueddach, K.; Schuster, A.; Becker, K.; Schiffer, P.; Holovachov, O.

items.title: CSF1R inhibition during cranial radiotherapy reshapes the immune environment and glial dynamics
items.abstract: Background: Cranial radiotherapy (cRT) induces long-lasting alterations in the brain microenvironment, including changes in glial populations and loss of neurogenesis. Pharmacological depletion of microglia via colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R) inhibition has been proposed as a strategy to modulate radiation-induced neuroinflammation, but its effects on other glial populations remains incompletely understood. Methods: Nine-week-old male C57BL/6JRj mice (n=60) received either a CSF1R-inhibitor supplemented diet (pexidartinib, PLX3397) or a control diet prior to and continued for 10 days after fractionated CT-guided cRT (3x10 Gy, 30 Gy). Brain tissue was assessed at multiple time-points up to six months post cRT using immunohistochemistry for markers of microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and proliferating cells. Microglial identity and repopulation dynamics were assessed using IBA1, F4/80 and the homeostatic microglial marker P2RY12, complemented by morphometric analysis. Results: Pexidartinib alone resulted in partial microglial depletion, whereas its combination with cRT led to near-complete loss of P2RY12+ homeostatic microglia at early time points. After discontinuation of the diet this was accompanied by increased IBA1+;F4/80high;P2RY12neg cell densities, consistent with replacement of the microglial niche by monocyte-derived cells. Over time, these cells exhibited gradual morphological adaptation but remained largely P2RY12neg, indicating incomplete restoration of a homeostatic microglial phenotype. Combined treatment accelerated astrocytic reactivity compared to cRT alone and did not prevent cRT-induced loss of neurogenesis or OPCs. At later time points, partial OPC recovery was observed in selected regions in the combined treatment group. Conclusion: CSF1R inhibition during cRT profoundly alters the composition and temporal dynamics of the brain its myeloid compartment, characterized by sustained loss of homeostatic microglia and replacement by monocyte-derived cells. Under these experimental conditions, microglial depletion did not mitigate key histopathological features associated with radiation-induced brain injury and was associated with accelerated astrocytic responses. These findings highlight the importance of timing, extent of depletion, and repopulation dynamics when considering microglia-targeting strategies in the context of cranial radiotherapy.
items.authors: Leter, Y. M.; van Heijningen, C. L.; Tolboom, Z. J.; de Gooijer, M. C.; Compter, A.; van Tellingen, O.; Schagen, S. B.; Kuil, L. E.

items.title: Evidence-Gated Plasticity and Context-Dependent Consolidation for Multi-Goal Learning in Spiking Neural Networks
items.abstract: Background / Introduction: Biologically inspired spiking neural networks offer a mechanistic framework for adaptive behavior, yet learning multiple goals remains challenging when synaptic updates for different targets interfere. We investigated whether multi-timescale plasticity and context-specific credit assignment improve interleaved multi-goal learning in a spiking navigation system inspired by entorhinal-hippocampal circuitry. Methods: We introduce evidence-gated plasticity (EGP), in which reward-modulated spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) generates transient synaptic proposals and need-weighted behavioral evidence modulates their slower consolidation into durable weights. Global EGP pools these proposals and the corresponding evidence across goals. Target-context EGP extends this framework through goal-specific proposal and evidence stores and additional need-dependent scaling of consolidation. We compared the algorithms across paired spiking networks, tested learned weights with plasticity disabled, and examined upstream representations and consolidation components. Results: Global EGP supported multi-goal learning and durable navigation. Target-context EGP improved early reward across 40 paired networks, including an independently specified 30-pair replication. Across eight paired networks trained for 2000 episodes, target-context EGP maintained a reward advantage, increased target-contact success, and reduced expected time to reach the target when unsuccessful blocks were included. Independent fixed-weight evaluation demonstrated durable navigation in both algorithms, with seven of eight networks favoring target-context EGP. A component experiment reproduced the target-context reward advantage and identified additional need-dependent scaling of context-specific consolidation as the only component with adjusted statistical support for improved reward. Conclusions: EGP supports durable multi-goal learning in spiking neural networks, and its target-context extension improves acquisition and conditional target selectivity in this interleaved navigation task. The framework offers a basis for testing context-sensitive, evidence-modulated plasticity in other multi-context learning problems.
items.authors: Neymotin, S. A.; Hazan, H.; Unal, G.; Earl, C.; Anwar, H.; Franaszczuk, P.; Boothe, D.

items.title: Hunger reconfigures a reward learning circuit into a memory competent mode
items.abstract: Internal states such as hunger dynamically reshape activity across circuits to support resource seeking. Neuromodulation provides a means of controlling such physiological properties of neurons, but how this flexibility regulates memory networks remains unclear. Here, we describe how hunger reconfigures a dopaminergic food-reward circuit between two physiological modes that support memory formation, in Drosophila. Starvation suppresses baseline dopaminergic activity through peptidergic signalling, enabling reward-evoked, large-amplitude dopamine neuron spikes to reinforce learning. This spiking mode can be engaged by sugar consumption and persists beyond feeding, reflecting the fly's satiety state. Persistent dopaminergic large-amplitude spiking reinforces learning and transitions the memory network into a mode that prioritizes consolidation of recently acquired memories. The transition from hunger to satiation is also reflected in the activity of postsynaptic output neurons that shift from a tonic, decorrelated mode that is responsive to dopamine into a bursting, correlated mode in which further dopaminergic modulation is occluded. Therefore, nutrient deprivation reconfigures the memory circuit into a learning competent dopamine-receptive mode, which persistent reinforcing dopamine then switches into a satiated mode driving memory consolidation. Together these processes mechanistically intertwine state-dependent reward-signalling with subsequent memory stabilization through transitions in physiological mode.
items.authors: Park, A.; Senapati, B.; Mancini, N.; Zhang, Y.; Choi, J.; Cone, I.; Treiber, C. D.; Costa, R. P.; Fenk, L. M.; Bidaye, S. S.; Waddell, S.

items.title: Cooperative cis-interactions between ectodomains of TCRαβ CD3 subunits enable mechanotransduction
items.abstract: TCR signaling poses a mechanical problem: pMHC binding occurs at the TCR{beta} ectodomain (ECD) head, whereas ITAM phosphorylation occurs on CD3 cytoplasmic tails. Chemistry cannot bridge this >10 nm gap, so the two events must be coupled through the TCR-CD3 interface, involving conformational allostery allowing force-based regulation. Although weak ECD cis-interactions between TCR{beta} and CD3 have been proposed to contribute to this coupling, their kinetics and mechanical competence remain elusive. Here, we quantify TCR{beta}-CD3 ECD cis-interactions in a pseudo-cis configuration by two-dimensional affinity and single-bond force spectroscopy, finding that TCR{beta}-CD3{gamma}{epsilon} and TCR{beta}-CD3{delta}{epsilon} bimolecular interactions have low affinity and rapid kinetics, yet form catch bonds. Critically, concurrent engagement of CD3{gamma}{epsilon} and CD3{delta}{epsilon} generates cis-cooperativity, yielding a stronger and longer-lasting CD3{gamma}{epsilon}-TCR{beta}-CD3{delta}{epsilon} trimolecular catch bond than the sum of the two dimeric bonds, with force-stabilized lifetimes matching those of agonist TCR-pMHC trans-interaction. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal an expanded, cooperative, and asymmetric contact network, making CD3{delta}{epsilon} more force-responsive and susceptible to conformational change than CD3{gamma}{epsilon}. Interface mutations do not alter force-free affinities but remodel force-dependent cis-bond profiles, leading to an inverse correlation with trans-bond profiles and T cell signaling. These results define cooperative ECD cis-interaction as a mechanically regulatable allosteric coupling element at the TCR-CD3 junction important to antigen recognition and signal initiation.
items.authors: Cong, P.; Natarajan, A.; Yuan, Z.; Ge, C.; Travaglino, S.; Dezhkam, R.; Beesam, S.; Li, X.; Grazette, D.; Krogsgaard, M.; Zhu, C.

items.title: A surviving beta cell subpopulation enriched in patients with T1D
items.abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is characterized by the autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells. While most beta cells are lost, a subset of beta cells persists years and even decades after disease onset. Studying these surviving cells is challenging, and thus how they escape immune killing remains poorly understood. Here, we applied a gene regulatory network inference-based clustering approach on existing islet scRNAseq data from cadaveric donors with T1D, autoantibody positive donors at risk for T1D, and non-diabetic donors to analyze beta cells from patients with established T1D. This approach identified a novel beta cell subtype enriched in T1D donors defined by the activity of several transcription factors which have well-characterized roles in beta cell survival, most notably IRF1. We found increased expression of immunomodulatory genes (e.g. SOCS1/3, HLA-E) as well as decreased expression of autoantigens and secretory genes, suggesting loss of cellular identity. We identified inflammatory cytokines as a driver of this phenotype by reanalyzing public data from primary human beta cells stimulated with inflammatory cytokines in vitro. We find a similar transcriptional program active in a subset of alpha cells, consistent with cell-extrinsic inflammatory cytokine signaling in vivo. We additionally use immunofluorescence to validate these findings. Overall, this study defines the features of surviving beta cells in patients with T1D, revealing several genes and pathways active in these cells as potential targets for T1D prevention and reversal.
items.authors: Spurrell, M.; Tobiasova, Z.; Pober, J. S.; Tsang, J.; Herold, K. C.

items.title: Relatedness of Gardnerella prophages and their endolysins
items.abstract: The Gardnerella genus includes a complex sub-taxonomy of bacterial species and subgroups which have been implicated in bacterial vaginosis. We analyzed G. leopoldii, G. swidsinski, G. piotii, and G. vaginalis genomes available in public databases and predicted proviral sequences using Cenote-Taker3. We clustered 266 prophage sequences into 140 viral genera level groupings that encode four distinct gene clusters and 19 different lysin proteins. Analysis of the bacterial and prophage sequence phylogenies reveals that while there were no specific prophage sequence lineages that infected each bacterial host, there is clustering of the prophage sequences by bacterial species within the Gardnerella genus.
items.authors: Maust, B. S.; Griswold, K. A.; Khim, M.; Subramanian, S.; Staker, B.; Myler, P. J.; Kullin, B. R.; Happel, A.-U.; Varsani, A.; Jaspan, H. B.

items.title: The staphylococcal type VII secretion system delays inflammatory cell death during macrophage infection
items.abstract: The human pathogen Staphylococcus aureus is a facultatively intracellular bacterium that can replicate and survive within macrophages. While macrophage-mediated immune modulation is pivotal in S. aureus pathogenesis, bacterial manipulation of macrophage pathways remains poorly understood. The specialised type VII secretion system (T7SSb) is an important virulence-associated factor during staphylococcal infection, although, unlike its mycobacterial counterparts, its role in controlling staphylococcal-macrophage interactions remains unclear. Employing high-resolution time-lapse imaging, we demonstrated an induction of pore-induced cellular traps (PITs) during S. aureus infection of macrophages in vitro, with a higher number of PITs forming in macrophages infected with S. aureus lacking EssC ({Delta}essC), a central T7SS transporter. Interestingly, {Delta}essC-infected macrophages displayed increased bacterial escape compared to wild type (WT)-infected cells, implicating a role for T7SS in delaying macrophage cell death. Changes in cell death were accompanied by a reduction in efferocytosis of {Delta}essC-infected cells in vitro. Investigation of cell death signalling markers in WT and {Delta}essC-infected macrophages demonstrated that the T7SS delayed induction of key cell death pathways, necroptosis and pyroptosis, and a dual RNAseq analysis of WT- and {Delta}essC-infected macrophages indicated a T7SS-dependent modulation of bacterial oxidative stress and selected host chemokines. We also demonstrated that T7SS effectors, EsxA and EsxC individually delayed macrophage cell death. Interestingly, {Delta}esxC mutants demonstrated accelerated calcium fluxes, indicating that the T7SS-mediated suppression of cellular calcium signalling may cause the delay in cell death. Furthermore, in a murine skin infection model, we showed that effector and transporter mutants have distinct S. aureus infection outcomes. Our findings suggest for the first time a key role for T7SSb proteins in controlling macrophage cell death, which impacts staphylococcal survival within the host during infection.
items.authors: Allen, R. D.; Farzand, R.; Chandrasekharan, G.; Watkins, K. E.; Agarwal, P.; Unnikrishnan, M.

items.title: Targeted Depletion of rRNAs and Tobamoviruses Enhances Viral Discovery in Wastewater Metatranscriptomes
items.abstract: Wastewater contains a complex mixture of nucleic acids derived from human cells, microorganisms, diets, and agricultural or industrial inputs. Metatranscriptomics has the potential to broaden the understanding of wastewater viromes, but its utility is constrained by high-abundance RNA molecules that prevent the detection of lower-abundance signals, including human pathogens. Two major sources of this interfering background signal are ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) from various organisms, and plant-infecting tobamoviruses from human diets, which are often the most abundant RNA viruses in wastewater. These rRNA molecules and RNA genomes can account for upwards of 95% of total RNA sequences, thereby obscuring the detection of lower-abundance viruses of public health importance. This study evaluated whether combined depletion of ribosomal RNAs and genomic RNA from abundant plant tobamoviruses can improve the recovery of underrepresented viral sequences from wastewater. RNA extracts from a large municipal wastewater treatment plant in Calgary, Canada, were processed with or without probe-based depletion of rRNAs and eight abundant tobamoviruses. Metatranscriptomes revealed that depletion reduced rRNA reads by 90%. Reads assigned to tobamoviruses, which accounted for up to 25% of viral reads in untreated samples, were reduced to <2% of viral reads after depletion. This decrease in undesired RNA signal led to an order of magnitude increase in viral read signals and improved assembled viral genome quality. Furthermore, the number of reads assigned to human and animal pathogens increased 42-fold after depletion, enabling the detection of important pathogens like influenza, RSV, and hepatitis A, which were undecteable in untreated samples. Together, these findings demonstrate that targeted depletion of abundant background RNAs improves the detection of low abundance viruses, and enhances the utility of metatranscriptomic approaches for wastewater viral surveillance.
items.authors: Bautista, M. A.; Bhardwaj, T.; Barbera, D. J.; Rulli, S. J.; Zorz, J.; McCalder, J.; Papparis, C.; Pang, X.; Lee, B. E.; Qiu, J.; Clark, R. G.; Acosta, N.; O' Grady, C.; Parkins, M. D.; Hubert, C. R.

items.title: Sequence-Dependent DNA Base Selection Fidelity: A Kinetics-Based Model and its Validation
items.abstract: DNA replication achieves error rates as low as 10-9-10-11 per base pair through the combined contribution of base selection, exonuclease proofreading, and mismatch repair. Among those processes, base selection determines the initial level of accuracy and is strongly modulated by local sequence context. Existing models address this dependence either by fitting individual rate constants for each sequence context or by invoking the global template properties, neither of which derives sequence dependence from the underlying thermodynamics and kinetics of base pair formation. Here we present a mechanism for sequence-dependent base selection fidelity, built from two physical properties: nearest-neighbor stacking thermodynamics and directional kinetic asymmetry. The model fits the experimentally observed mutation spectra from three mismatch repair-deficient organisms well (r=0.74, 0.70, and 0.63), and predicts that base-selection accuracy varies non-monotonically with temperature in a sequence-dependent manner. Our model, therefore, provides a framework that connects sequence-dependent thermodynamic and kinetic effects during nucleotide incorporation to experimentally observed mutation rates.
items.authors: Ghosh, K.; Sahu, P.; Barik, S.; Subramanian, H.

items.title: EventHorizon: A Foundation Model for Clinical Flow Cytometry
items.abstract: Clinical flow cytometry is central to diagnosing hematologic malignancies, but its reliance on manual expert interpretation and fixed panel designs limits scalability and adaptability. To address this, we developed EventHorizon, a self-supervised foundation model that combines a hierarchical, marker-aware transformer with self-distillation pre-training. EventHorizon integrates heterogeneous, multi-tube panels into a unified, specimen-level embedding. Pre-trained without labels on 100,937 routine clinical specimens, comprising over 50 billion cells, the model yields frozen embeddings that enable lightweight classifiers to accurately identify recurrent genetic abnormalities in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), including t(15;17) (AUROC 0.991) and an unexpected signal for DDX41 mutations (AUROC 0.970). EventHorizon maintained strong performance on a temporally separated 2026 cohort (macro AUROC 0.970 across 28 diagnoses) and demonstrated zero-shot transferability across a five-site B-cell lymphoma cohort (CLL vs. normal AUROC 0.988), the FlowCAP-II AML challenge (AUROC 0.973), and B-ALL measurable residual disease detection (AUROC 0.920 at [ ]1% disease burden). Although class ranking transferred reliably across sites, decision thresholds shifted; however, these were rapidly recalibrated using as few as four labeled AML cases. Sensitivity decreased at disease burdens below 0.1%, yet embeddings remained robust to simulated assay perturbations. Overall, EventHorizon offers a reusable, panel-agnostic representation for diagnostic flow cytometry.
items.authors: Medina Grespan, M.; Morrison, M.; O'Fallon, B.; Jacobsen, J. R.; Shean, R. C.; Spies, N. C.; Ng, D.

items.title: The CAHRA Challenge: A Community-Wide Assessment of Cryo-EM Heterogeneous Reconstruction Algorithms
items.abstract: The ability of cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to interrogate the atomic structure and motion of biomolecules has motivated the development of a wide range of algorithms for heterogeneity analysis. However, evaluating and comparing these methods remains challenging because ground-truth structures are generally unknown for experimental samples. Here, we introduce the 2026 Community-Wide Assessment of Heterogeneous Reconstruction Algorithms (CAHRA), a community-wide challenge centered on three benchmark datasets that probe distinct tasks in heterogeneity analysis. These include (1) compositional heterogeneity arising from mixtures of distinct protein complexes, (2) continuous conformational variability and atomic modeling, and (3) entanglement between molecular conformation and particle pose. We describe the design, construction, and validation of these datasets, as well as their use in the recently completed CAHRA Challenge.
items.authors: Feathers, J. R.; Heeter, R.; Woollard, G.; Hanson, S. M.; Cossio, P.; Greer, J.; Burnley, T.; Zhong, E.

items.title: The Red Blood Cell Surface Defines a Distinct Tumor DNA Compartment for Liquid Biopsy
items.abstract: Red blood cells (RBCs) modulate host inflammatory responses by scavenging mitochondrial and pathogen DNA. However, how RBC surface properties govern the capture of tumor-derived DNA remains poorly understood. We show that RBCs tether and retain tumor-derived DNA on their surface, forming a distinct circulating pool of RBC-bound tumor DNA (rtDNA). Desialylation increased DNA capture in a Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9)-dependent manner, identifying RBC surface sialylation and TLR9 as a regulator of DNA binding. In mice bearing lung cancer xenografts, rtDNA was detected in all animals and its abundance correlated with tumor burden, whereas tumor DNA was undetectable in matched plasma samples. In patients with lung cancer, the majority of detected mutant tumor DNA was associated with RBCs rather than plasma, and RBC-derived mutations were concordant with molecular alterations identified in matched tumor tissue. Collectively, these findings establish the RBC surface as a tunable site of tumor-DNA capture and retention and challenge the plasma-centric paradigm of liquid biopsy by identifying a distinct cellular reservoir of tumor-derived genetic material.
items.authors: Elias, E.; Ruger, H.; Predina, J.; Bleiberg, B. A.; Noguera-Ortega, E.; Areesawangkit, P.; Kulkarni, A.; Thompson, J. C.; Shashaty, M. G. S.; Langer, C.; Albelda, S. M.; Mangalmurti, N. S.

items.title: Acclimation capacity of two-banded seabream juveniles (Diplodus vulgaris) to port conditions: implications for the role of ports as nursery habitats
items.abstract: orts are highly anthropized coastal environments characterized by elevated pollution and habitat alteration, posing significant challenges for marine organisms. However, the effects of port conditions on juvenile coastal fish using ports as nurseries remain poorly understood. Here, we combined field sampling and in situ caging experiments to investigate the genetic structure (RAD-seq), physiological condition (growth, lipid content, CYP1A-dependent biotransformation activity), and transcriptomic responses (RNA-seq) of juvenile two-banded sea bream (Diplodus vulgaris) exposed to port conditions. Juveniles from a port site were compared with individuals from two nearby non-port sites (T0), before fish from all populations were caged within the port for one month (T1). The site furthest from the port was slightly genetically differentiated. Port juveniles were larger and fatter at T0 than fish from non-port populations, and all populations showed differential regulation of lipid metabolism, xenobiotic detoxification, hypoxia response, and circadian rhythm pathways between T0 and T1. After one month of caging, weight differences persisted while muscle lipid content sharply declined in all populations. Only juveniles from the site furthest from the port significantly grew between T0 and T1. Port juveniles had a different transcriptional response to caging than non-port juveniles, with a higher expression of genes associated with energy metabolism, while non-port individuals overexpressed genes in detoxification, lipid metabolism, and oncogenic pathways. While we admit limitations related to caging conditions, our results suggest that port conditions strongly influence juvenile fish physiology and transcriptional levels, potentially promoting short-term acclimation strategies that could have long-term consequences for health and survival.
items.authors: Reisser, C. M.; Rapp, M.; Farcy, E.; Blondeau-Bidet, E.; Cornette, F.; Mahe, K.; Bouchoucha, M.

items.title: Cell cycle exit is required for differentiation and cell fate diversification but not neoblast specialisation in planarians
items.abstract: In planarians, adult stem cells constantly proliferate and differentiate into dozens of different cell types to maintain tissue homeostasis. However, how cell fate acquisition is coordinated with cell cycle progression remains poorly understood. To address this, we generated single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets from cells enriched for 2C or 4C DNA content and from animals subjected to RNAi against the cell cycle regulators cdh1 and h2b. We found that progenitor populations from multiple lineages contain actively cycling cells enriched in the 4C state. Cell fate acquisition to most cell types is acquired progressively during neoblast differentiation. Comparative analysis of cell cycle regulators confirmed a simplified regulatory repertoire in Schmidtea, supporting a central role for cdh1 in controlling cell cycle exit. RNAi-mediated knockdown of cdh1 caused homeostasis defects, impaired regeneration, accumulation of neoblasts and depletion of progenitors. Together, our findings demonstrate that cell cycle exit is required for terminal differentiation but not for neoblast specialisation. Instead, lineage commitment is initiated in actively cycling neoblasts, whereas terminal differentiation depends on cdh1-mediated cell cycle exit.
items.authors: Peron, S.; Balta, O.-M.; Noronha, A.; Smillie, T.; Mason, V.; Perez-Posada, A.; Solana, J.

items.title: The dentate gyrus controls hippocampal representational drift
items.abstract: Neural representations evolve across time and experience, a phenomenon termed representational drift. The function and circuit mechanisms of drift remain unknown, including whether it reflects intrinsic biological variability within the population or is actively controlled by circuit inputs. Progress has been limited because there is currently no known experimental means to manipulate drift without also altering an animal's sensory or behavioral experience. Here we show that drift can be experimentally controlled through targeted manipulation of upstream circuit inputs. We demonstrate this principle in the hippocampus by selectively manipulating dentate gyrus granule cells, which are thought to promote discrimination between similar experiences. Inhibiting granule cells during repeated experiences in familiar virtual environments markedly reduced drift in downstream CA1, revealing that representational drift is not simply an intrinsic property of neural populations, but is actively controlled by upstream circuitry. By experimentally manipulating this circuit-level control of drift, we further discovered that hippocampal drift is concentrated around episode transitions rather than accumulating continuously throughout an experience. These findings establish experimental control over hippocampal drift, revealing a structured, circuit-regulated process that differentiates repeated experiences into distinct episodic representations.
items.authors: GoodSmith, D.; Madar, A.; Carson, W. H.; Sheffield, M. E.

items.title: Renin, Major Adverse Cardiovascular Outcomes, and the Use of Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists in Hypertension
items.abstract: Background: The prognostic significance of renin activity and its role in identifying patients who may benefit from mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) remain incompletely defined. Methods: In a multicentre retrospective cohort of 16,600 adults with hypertension, we evaluated associations between baseline plasma renin activity and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), comprising ischaemic stroke, intracranial haemorrhage, myocardial infarction, and all-cause death. Renin was analysed using restricted cubic splines and categories. Time-dependent Cox models assessed associations between MRA use and outcomes across renin strata, treating MRA exposure as time-varying. Findings: Renin showed a U-shaped association with MACE, with the lowest estimated risk at 1.17 ng/mL/h. Compared with renin 0.3-.0 ng/mL/h, both low renin ( 3.0 ng/mL/h; HR 1.19, 1.06-1.33) were associated with higher MACE risk. MRA use was associated with lower MACE risk when renin was low ( 3.0 ng/mL/h [1.07, 0.76-1.52]). MRA use was associated with lower all-cause mortality across renin categories [ ]3.0 ng/mL/h, whereas no significant association was observed at renin >3.0 ng/mL/h. Interpretation: Baseline renin showed a U-shaped association with MACE. The use of MRAs was associated with lower risk of MACE only when renin was low. These findings provide support for renin-guided MRA therapy in hypertension.
items.authors: Tsai, C.-H.; Chang, Y.-C.; Chang, C.-C.; Newman, A. J.; Brown, J.; Wu, V.-C.; Lin, Y.-H.; Vaidya, A.

items.title: WALK for Freezing of Gait in Parkinson's Disease: A Sham-Controlled Home Rehabilitation Trial
items.abstract: Background: Freezing of gait (FOG) in Parkinson disease often persists despite dopaminergic treatment. WALK is a bilateral thigh-worn device that delivers local muscle-tendon vibration during walking. We examined whether WALK could be incorporated into supervised home rehabilitation and explored differences in freezing severity between active and sham treatment. Methods: In this single-centre pilot randomised clinical trial, adults with Parkinson disease and neurologist-confirmed FOG were assigned to Active or Sham-WALK. Both groups completed the same 16-session, six-week supervised home programme; mZ-FOG was assessed in the medication OFF state at baseline and after sessions 8 and 16. At each follow-up, assessment without the device preceded assessment with the assigned device. The complete-case analysis tested the Group X Condition interaction across the five conditions. Trial registration: Clinical Trials Registry-India, CTRI/2022/01/039256, https://ctri.nic.in/; registered 7 January 2022. Results: Ninety people were screened, 47 were randomised (active, n=27; sham, n=20), and 40 completed follow-up and entered the main analysis (active, n=24; sham, n=16). Retention was 85.1% (95% CI 74.9% to 95.4%), and all completers finished the 16-session programme. No serious device-related adverse event was reported among completers; one active-group participant discontinued because of fatigue. mZ-FOG scores decreased in both groups, but the Group X Condition interaction was not significant (F=0.847, p=0.465). At S16 before device reapplication, the baseline-adjusted active-minus-sham difference was -2.98 points (95% CI -6.63 to 0.66; p=0.106); with the assigned device, it was -2.87 points (95% CI -6.76 to 1.02; p=0.144). In the Active-WALK group, 18 of 24 improved by at least the 4.28-point MCID. Conclusion: WALK was feasible to integrate into supervised home rehabilitation and was associated with improvement in freezing across training. The lower active-group score before device reapplication at S16 suggests that improvement may have extended beyond the period of immediate stimulation.
items.authors: Benny, R.; Desai, A.; Venkitachalam, A.; Thakkar, V.; Rajput, R.; Chakrabarty, S.

items.title: A Zero-Shot Decision Model (Jev) Matches a Trained Classifier but Ranks Its Own Errors Worse: Calibrated, Split-Conformal Next-Procedure Recommendation in General Dentistry
items.abstract: On real-world dental records, procedure history predicts the next procedure category well, and a simple history-aware classical model beats every large-language-model (LLM) design we tested. We study the question that follows every dental diagnosis: given a patients chart and most recent procedure, what should the dentist do next? Commercial dental artificial intelligence in 2026 is overwhelmingly diagnostic, and the closest published system for this sequencing task, MultiTP (Chen et al., 2024b), offers neither calibrated uncertainty, structured rationale, nor an evaluation as decision support. We introduce DentaCoPilot, a recommender that returns a calibrated top-K distribution over Current Dental Terminology (CDT) codes, a verbalised confidence label, an explicit abstain flag, and a chart-grounded rationale, and we compare four classical baselines with six LLM variants. On an apples-to-apples synthetic evaluation, classical baselines reach 0.567 top-1 while pure LLM variants trail at 0.267 to 0.467, and moving the backbone from Sonnet to Opus does not help. Prompt-conditioning a Sonnet LLM on the classical baselines candidate list closes most of the gap while preserving rationale and abstention; because the synthetic generator shares Markov structure with the bigram baseline, these synthetic rankings index pipeline behaviour, not externally valid clinical performance. We anchor external validity for the task on the public MEPS 2023 corpus (11,016 next-visit transitions across 5,088 patients): a history-aware model reaches 0.479 top-1 against 0.297 for a most-frequent baseline, is well calibrated (expected calibration error 0.031), and supports split-conformal selective prediction with a distribution-free coverage guarantee. A zero-shot LLM given only 1 this coarse history loses to the same classical baseline, so the LLMs value depends on rich charts rather than category history alone. Prospective clinician-in-the-loop validation and CDT-level real-data validation remain future work, contingent on clinical-data access and ethics approval that we have sought but not secured.
items.authors: Rodrigues, C. C.; Rebello, S. D.

items.title: PRE-CISE: A PRE-calibration Coverage, Identifiability, and SEnsitivity analysis workflow to streamline model calibration
items.abstract: PurposeWe introduce PRE-CISE, a pre-calibration workflow integrating coverage analysis, local sensitivity, and collinearity diagnostics to streamline model calibration. We demonstrate PRE-CISEs benefits using two testbeds (a Sick-Sicker Markov model and an SIR transmission model) and a COVID-19 case study. MethodsPRE-CISE uses coverage analysis to verify that model outputs generated from the prior distribution span calibration targets, followed by local sensitivities to quantify parameter influence, guiding the resizing of prior bounds to improve coverage. Identifiability is assessed via collinearity analysis; large indices indicate practical nonidentifiability. Bayesian calibration was used: for the testbed models (3 and 2 parameters, respectively) to match their targets; for the COVID-19 model (11 parameters) to match daily confirmed incident cases. ResultsCoverage analyses flagged initial misfits; local sensitivities identified that the Sick-to-Sicker transition probability has a greater effect on model outputs, and resizing its prior distribution bounds improved coverage. Collinearity analyses indicated that using multiple calibration targets over different time points enabled identification of all three parameters. For the SIR testbed, collinearity indices declined as target points accumulated, crossing the identifiability threshold once the data spanned the epidemic peak. In the COVID-19 model, local sensitivity analyses prioritized time-varying detection rates and contact-reduction effects, reducing the search space. Daily incident case calibration targets yielded collinearity indices below practical thresholds for all parameter combinations, whereas indices for weekly calibration targets were larger. PRE-CISE achieved greater calibration efficiency gains for denser posterior sampling and more complex models. ConclusionsPRE-CISE provides a practical, transparent pathway that helps modelers refine prior distribution bounds and calibration targets before intensive calibration, improving uncertainty reporting and strengthening the reliability of model-based health policy analyses.
items.authors: Gracia, V.; Goldhaber-Fiebert, J. D.; Alarid-Escudero, F.

items.title: The lingering legacy: Resilience as a pathway linking retrospective organisational support and police retirement adjustment
items.abstract: This study evaluated retirement adjustment in UK retired police officers (N = 289) across two analytical models. The moderation model revealed a non-significant overall interaction, though exploratory Johnson-Neyman analysis identified an emergent region at 32.07 years post-retirement, where perceived organisational support significantly predicted adjustment. This suggests a long-term organisational legacy effect, wherein retrospective perceptions of service value serve as a durable psychological resource in later life. Conversely, the mediation model confirmed psychological resilience as a significant statistical mediator directly linking support to adjustment. The findings support lifelong post-service wellbeing strategies, as organisational relationships influence adjustment decades after retirement.
items.authors: Vaportzis, E.; Edwards, W.

items.title: Skeletal muscle enhancer programming of intrinsic cardiorespiratory fitness
items.abstract: Cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) is a heritable trait associated with improved metabolic health and longevity. Integrating 546 transcriptomic and epigenomic profiles from skeletal muscle of 128 genetically heterogeneous rats selectively bred for high and low running capacity (HCR and LCR), a model that mirrors CRF-associated traits in humans, we identify a distributed enhancer architecture underlying their divergent transcriptomes. Line-divergent alleles were concentrated in distal enhancers: those more active in HCR were enriched for ETS-family transcription factor motifs and positively linked to hundreds of mitochondrial oxidative metabolism and angiogenesis genes, whereas those more active in LCR were enriched for Mef2 motifs and negatively linked to these genes. In 426 genotype, gene expression, and chromatin accessibility profiles from an independent HCRxLCR F2 population (n=147), we validated thousands of these genetic effects. Thus, heritable CRF reflects many enhancers cumulatively tuning energy metabolism and oxygen delivery, providing a molecular basis for variation in CRF.
items.authors: Weitzel, A. M.; Orchard, P.; Evans, C.; Manickam, N.; Treutelaar, M. K.; Britton, S. L.; Koch, L. G.; Li, J. Z.; Parker, S. C. J.; Burant, C. F.

items.title: Design of Orthogonal Far-Red, Orange and Green Fluorophore-binding Proteins for Multiplex Imaging
items.abstract: Fluorescent proteins have transformed biological imaging, yet their limited photostability and brightness restrict their applications. We used deep learning-based de novo protein design methods to design binders to three bright, stable and cell-permeable dyes spanning the imaging spectrum: JF657 (far red), JF596 (orange-red) and JF494 (green). We obtain highly specific dye-binding proteins with low nanomolar affinities for the intended target; a crystal structure of one binder confirms close resemblance to the design model. Simultaneous labeling of mammalian cells expressing three dye-specific binders at different subcellular compartments demonstrates the utility in multiplex imaging. We further expand the functionality of the binder by incorporating an active site that carries out nucleophilic aromatic substitution to form a covalent linkage with the dye, and develop split versions which reconstitute fluorescence at subcellular locations where both halves are present towards monitoring in-cell protein interactions and chemically induced dimerization. Our designed high affinity and specificity dye binders open up new opportunities for multiplexed biological imaging.
items.authors: Tran, L.; Klein, S.; Sharma, S.; Juergens, D.; Decarreau, J.; Liu, B.; Wang, Y.; Bera, A. K.; Kang, A.; Woods, J.; Joyce, E.; Vafeados, D. K.; Roullier, N.; Chen, W.; Lee, G. R.; Lavis, L. D.; Mahamid, J.; An, L.; Baker, D.
items.title_zh: 正交远红、橙色和绿色荧光染料结合蛋白的设计用于多重成像
items.summary_zh: 荧光蛋白已改变生物成像，但其有限的光稳定性和亮度限制了应用。我们采用基于深度学习的全新蛋白设计方法，设计了三种明亮、稳定且可穿透细胞的染料结合蛋白，分别对应于成像光谱中的JF657（远红）、JF596（橙红）和JF494（绿色）。我们获得了对目标染料具有低纳摩尔亲和力的高特异性结合蛋白；其中一个结合蛋白的晶体结构确认与设计模型高度相似。通过同时标记表达三种染料特异性结合蛋白的哺乳动物细胞在不同亚细胞区室中的应用，展示了其在多重成像中的实用性。我们进一步通过引入一个活性位点，进行亲核芳香取代反应与染料形成共价连接，扩展了结合蛋白的功能，并开发了在亚细胞位置重组荧光的分裂版本，以监测细胞内蛋白相互作用和化学诱导的二聚化。我们设计的高亲和力和高特异性染料结合蛋白为多重生物成像开辟了新机遇。
items.l1_lead: 通过深度学习设计的三种新型荧光染料结合蛋白，具备高亮度和稳定性，推动了多重生物成像技术的发展。
items.l2_summary:
荧光蛋白的出现极大地推动了生物成像技术的发展，但其光稳定性和亮度的局限性仍然制约了其广泛应用。为了解决这一问题，研究团队采用基于深度学习的全新蛋白设计方法，成功设计出三种明亮、稳定且能够穿透细胞的染料结合蛋白，分别对应于成像光谱中的JF657（远红）、JF596（橙红）和JF494（绿色）。这些结合蛋白展现出对目标染料的低纳摩尔亲和力和高特异性，且其中一个结合蛋白的晶体结构与设计模型高度相似，验证了设计的有效性。

在实验中，研究人员通过同时标记表达这三种染料特异性结合蛋白的哺乳动物细胞，展示了其在不同亚细胞区室中的应用，进一步证明了这些结合蛋白在多重成像中的实用性。此外，研究团队还通过引入一个活性位点，进行亲核芳香取代反应与染料形成共价连接，扩展了结合蛋白的功能。这一创新使得研究人员能够开发出在亚细胞位置重组荧光的分裂版本，从而监测细胞内蛋白相互作用和化学诱导的二聚化。

总体而言，研究团队设计的高亲和力和高特异性染料结合蛋白为多重生物成像开辟了新的机遇，推动了生物成像技术的进一步发展。这些成果不仅为基础生物学研究提供了强有力的工具，也为未来的生物医学应用奠定了基础。

items.title: Dysfunctional effector programming in Foxp3-ΔE2 Tregs promotes enhanced CD8+ T cell responses
items.abstract: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) prevent autoimmunity through suppressive functions largely programmed by the transcription factor FOXP3. Humans express two major alternatively spliced isoforms of FOXP3: a full-length version containing all coding exons (FOXP3-FL) and a version lacking Exon 2 (FOXP3-{Delta}E2). Sole FOXP3-{Delta}E2 expression causes lethal IPEX syndrome, indicating that FOXP3 Exon 2 is essential for full Treg function. Here, we used Foxp3-{Delta}E2 mice to determine how Foxp3 Exon 2 impacts the functional differentiation of Tregs at homeostasis and during inflammation. Analysis of central and effector Foxp3-{Delta}E2 Treg populations revealed dysfunctional effector Treg programming, including reduced expression of IL-2 receptor subunits, CTLA-4, and tissue-homing chemokine receptors. During influenza infection, reduced IL-2 regulation by Foxp3-{Delta}E2 Tregs and decreased Foxp3-{Delta}E2 Treg localization to the T cell zone during priming contributed to enhanced acute and memory CD8+ T cell responses. Thus, dysfunctional effector Treg programming by the Foxp3-{Delta}E2 isoform impairs suppressive function, resulting in failure to restrain CD8+ T cells and aberrant immune responses.
items.authors: Weinstein, K. N.; Bishop, Z. H.; Shamskhou, E. A.; Barry, F. N.; Verdezoto, G.; de Leon, M.; Albe, J. R.; Koval, A.; Zhou, B.; Domeier, P. P.; Gerner, M. Y.; Campbell, D. J.; Ziegler, S. F.

items.title: Combined High Fat and Viral Insults in Pregnancy Disrupt Specific Placental Nutrient Transporter Systems in Mice
items.abstract: The placenta adapts to support nutrient transport to meet the demands of the growing fetus. Maternal obesity and viral infection are associated with adverse fetoplacental development. How co-exposure affects placental morphology and nutrient transport across gestation remains unclear. We hypothesise that co-exposure would have a greater impact on placental morphology and nutrient transporter expression than either of the exposures alone. C57BL/6J mice were fed a control (CON) or high-fat (HF) diet before and throughout pregnancy and exposed to poly(I:C) or vehicle at gestational days (GD) 12.5, 15.5, or 18.5. Placental morphology, folate and fatty acid transporter mRNA expression and localisation were evaluated by haematoxylin and eosin staining, immunohistochemistry (reported as % immunoreactivity (ir)-area stained), and qPCR, respectively. At GD12.5, HF diet associated with reduced junctional zone (JZ) area and increased maternal blood space, followed by reduced fetal blood space at GD15.5 and increased JZ and labyrinth zone (LZ) area size by GD18.5.
