The rate response of planar and structured DIW electrodes was analysed using a master-curve approach in which the model parameters were expressed as functions of active-material mass loading. This enabled a fair comparison between 2D and 3D electrodes minimizing the influence of structurally derived differences in thickness and intrinsic cell-to-cell variability. Throughout a wide selection of mass loadings, the 3D electrodes consistently showed improved rate performance. At the highest investigated mass loading, the structured electrodes exhibited capacity improvements above 20% at 2.7C, while showing a significant enhancement in power performance, particularly at high rates. These results demonstrate that the benefits of electrode structuring can be quantified as functions of both mass loading and operating conditions through the master-curve framework, providing a robust basis for evaluating and optimizing 3D electrode architectures.
items.authors: Tomás García Rodríguez, Sergio Pinilla

items.title: Active synthesizability prediction for a virtual space of 395 million catalyst candidates with small data
items.abstract: N-heterocyclic carbenes (NHCs) are well established as catalysts and ligands in many chemical transformations. Recently, interest has grown in pyridine[1,5]imidazolium salt pre-catalysts, stable precursors to NHCs, because they are relatively easy to synthesize and highly adaptable. This work introduces a data-driven workflow to identify which pyridine[1,5]imidazolium salts are readily synthetically accessible, starting from exploratory synthesis attempts for 127 compounds. Our approach relies on a feedback loop with a supervised machine learning model to estimate and dynamically update the synthesizability for a combinatorial space of about 394 million pre-catalysts derived from commercially available precursors. Our final model estimates that 4.78% of the entire space are feasible, mapping the space of readily accessible candidates and providing a valuable set for future inverse design studies. We validated the prediction performance of our approach based on both literature data and a holdout set occupying extremes of the combinatorial space.
items.authors: Hannes Hovorka, Noa Huismann, Yanchao Wang, Gian-Michele Cherchi, Michael Lesa, Shiquan Zhou

items.title: Atomic memory in molecular charge evolution in deep inner-shell Auger cascades.
items.abstract: A single low-keV X-ray photon can strip a molecule of more than ten electrons. Deep inner-shell ionization of heavy atoms, including those incorporated into radiosensitizers in emerging cancer therapies, initiates an Auger cascade that rapidly builds up high charge and can drive extensive fragmentation. How this charge accumulates, not the total energy deposited alone, governs the molecular response to irradiation. Yet cascade-driven charge buildup is neglected in current radiation-damage and dosimetry models because complex Auger cascades remain poorly understood, and tracing how this initially local atomic process develops into an extended molecular response remains challenging. We demonstrate that the total charge produced by an Auger cascade is already encoded in the first Auger decay step, which can be described using existing atomic data. State-selective Auger-electron–ion coincidence measurements on atomic xenon resolve this earliest branching and reveal markedly different final charge distributions, with mean charges ranging from +4 to +11 depending on the first Auger decay channel. In molecules, the later cascade is strongly modified by the surrounding valence-electron environment. Measurements on molecular iodine show substantially enhanced charge buildup, which is captured by an “ideal electron-reservoir model” representing how sustained access to valence electrons increases both the final charge and electron emission. Together, these results connect the intrinsically atomic first Auger decay step to the final molecular charge buildup and provide a route to include cascade-driven charging in predictive descriptions of X-ray damage, from structural biology to emerging Auger therapies.
items.authors: O. Travnikova, A. P. Chaynikov, H. Hartikainen, K.–I. Pusa, M. Berholts, D. Céolin

items.title: Kinetic Target-Guided Discovery of Selective Nanomolar Hydroxamic Acid–Based Inhibitors of Pseudomonas aeruginosa Elastase LasB
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is increasingly becoming a critical threat to human health. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is classified as a high-priority pathogen, and treating it with traditional antibiotics is increasingly challenging. In this work, we report on a non-traditional approach: targeting Elastase B, a major virulence factor that drives P. aeruginosa pathogenicity. Guided by prior crystallographic data, we employed a kinetic target-guided synthesis (KTGS) approach followed by an extensive structure–activity relationship (SAR) study, leading to the identification of inhibitors with single-digit nanomolar inhibitory potency (IC50= 1.7 ± 0.1 nM). These compounds also displayed excellent selectivity against a panel of human off-targets, protected lung epithelial cells from LasB-associated damage, and showed encouraging in vivo efficacy. Moreover, pulmonary pharmacokinetic studies revealed ELF and lung exposure above the biochemical IC50 values, supporting their further development as antivirulence agents against P. aeruginosa lung infections.
items.authors: Virgyl Camberlein, Angeliki Vgenopoulou, Alaa Alhayek, Roya Shafiei, Asfandyar Sikandar, Andreas Klein

items.title: Processing–structure–property relationships of Y2O3- and ZnO-modified MgO–Al2O3–SiO2 glasses for high-modulus fiber drawing
items.abstract: Magnesium aluminosilicate (MAS) glasses are attractive candidates for high-modulus (HM) reinforcing fibres but are prone to crystallisation, which restricts the usable forming window. Four MAS compositions modified with Y2O3 (T9, V9) or a combined Y 2 O 3 /ZnO addition (T10, V10) were investigated on a single experimental platform to define the window for crystallisation-free fibre drawing. Two base glasses were compared: an MgO-rich, Al 2 O 3 -lean variant (T series) and an Al 2 O 3 -rich, MgO-lean variant (V series). Compositions were verified by ICP-OES/MS, and characterised by dilatometry, DSC, rotational viscometry with Vogel–Fulcher–Tammann fits, gradient-furnace liquidus measurement and X-ray diffraction. The V series shows a glass transition 30–40 K above the T series and a 20 % lower thermal expansion coefficient. Substituting half of the Y 2 O 3 by ZnO lowers the glass transition by 13–30 K and raises the liquidus of the Al 2 O 3 -rich base from 1311 to 1340 °C. The DSC crystallisation onset lies a near-constant 33–37 K above the glass transition across all four glasses, indicating a kinetic barrier set by the MAS network rather than by the modifiers. All four were drawn into fully amorphous continuous fibres from nozzle temperatures only 40–69 K above their liquidus, and remain calorimetrically indistinguishable from the parent glass; V10, drawn 40 K above the highest liquidus, is the most stringent case. Crystallisation-free forming is therefore controlled by the rapid quench inherent to filament drawing rather than by a positive thermodynamic margin. The results support Y 2 O 3 -rich, Al 2 O 3 -rich compositions for HM-MAS fibre scale-up.
items.authors: Muawia Dafir, Holger Cebulla, Martin Kilo

items.title: Möbius Kekulene
items.abstract: Encoding prescribed topologies in rigid conjugated frameworks offers a route to tuning electronic properties but is constrained by severe geometric strain. We synthesized and isolated Möbius kekulene, a compact, all-benzenoid double-stranded counterpart of planar kekulene. Its synthesis was enabled by strain-trajectory programming, in which precursor connectivity is designed to control strain accumulation during cyclization. Comparison of two precursors revealed contrasting strain trajectories: MCP1 concentrated the torsional deformation into an inaccessible late-stage closure, whereasMCP2 accommodated deformation progressively, reducing the largest strain increment and affording Möbius kekulene 1. Crystallography confirms a singly twisted topology with a calculated strain energy of 73.9 kcal/mol per twist, highest among reported Möbius π-systems. Despite pronounced distortion, 1 retains a Clar-type localized electronic structure analogous to planar kekulene, with local aromaticity progressively perturbed toward the twist region. These results establish strain-trajectory programming as a design principle for accessing highly constrained molecular topologies.
items.authors: Mingxin He, Yong Ni

items.title: Iso-co-humulone Does Not Necessarily Contribute to the Roughness of Beer Bitterness
items.abstract: [Conclusion] Iso-co-humulone does not necessarily contribute to the roughness of beer bitterness. The long-repeated rule that a high cohumulone proportion produces rough, harsh, or lingering bitterness should not be accepted as a general law of brewing and should not be used by itself to judge hop quality or to predict the sensory quality of beer. [Background] The cohumulone–roughness hypothesis has been reproduced for decades in brewing literature, referenceworks, trainingmaterials, andhop-selectionpractice, despite limiteddirect evidence and timeintensity findings inconsistentwith a simple universal rule. This persistence is consequential: brewers, particularly those entering the field, may reject otherwise suitable hops or misdiagnose rough bitterness solely from a cohumulone specification. [Methods] Fractions containing iso-co-humulone, iso-normal-humulone, or iso-ad-humulone (each combining its cis and trans forms) were added separately to unhopped beer at 25 BU. Lingering bitter aftertaste was evaluated blind by six trained panelists on a nine-point anchored scale and by a lipid-membrane taste-sensing system. In a separate 3,000-L brewing comparison, the iso-co-humulone proportion was increased from 28.2% to 39.8%; eight trained panelists performed blind paired comparisons of lingering aftertaste and bitterness crispness (kire). [Results]Mean lingering-bitterness scores were 4.9, 6.2, and 6.9 for iso-co-humulone, iso-normal-humulone, and iso-ad-humulone, respectively. Corresponding taste-sensor aftertaste responses were 0.24, 2.89, and 2.73. In the brewing comparison, aftertaste choices were divided 4:4, whereas seven of eight panelists selected the higheriso-co-humulone beer as having greater crispness (one-sided exact p = 0.035; two-sided p = 0.070). [Interpretation] Roughness was not measured as a separate multidimensional attribute, and the brewing comparison was not independently replicated. Nevertheless, the convergent model-beer, sensor, and brewing observations contradict the necessary-persistence premise of the traditional roughness rule and do not justify treating a high iso-co-humulone proportion as automatic evidence of rough beer bitterness. A cohumulone percentage on a hop specification is not a sensory verdict.
items.authors: Toru KISHIMOTO

items.title: Solid-state NMR and first-principle calculations reveal the structure and dynamics of Li-N-H materials
items.abstract: Lithium-nitrogen-hydrogen (Li-N-H) materials are promising for hydrogen storage, solid-state batteries, and lithium-mediated ammonia synthesis, yet their local structures and proton dynamics remain poorly understood because of compositional disorder and limited sensitivity of conventional diffraction methods. Here, we combine multinuclear solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H, 7Li, 14N, and 15N ssNMR) with first-principles calculations to resolve the atomic environments and dynamics of Li3N, LiNH2, and Li1+xNH2-x (. 7Li NMR and density functional theory calculations identify distinct lithium sites in coexisting α- and β-Li3N phases and in tetragonal LiNH2. 1H and 15N NMR, together with 1H-detected 14N spectroscopy, reveal two distinct domains in synthesized lithium-rich Li1+xNH2-x that are not resolved by laboratory X-ray diffraction. Comparison with calculated NMR parameters assigns these domains to LiNH2 and Li2NH, respectively. Variable-temperature 1H-1H exchange spectroscopy shows that correlations between the two domains arise predominantly from spin diffusion rather than interdomain proton exchange, indicating nanoscale structural heterogeneity within a solid solution. Local proton motion occurs within the Li2NH environment and is restricted in the LiNH­2 domains. These results establish a molecular-level relationship between local structure and proton mobility in Li-N-H materials, providing insights relevant to hydrogen storage, solid-state batteries, and ammonia synthesis.
items.authors: Ruipeng Luo, Jennifer S. Gómez, Tom Speelman, Benjamin Tatman, Paul Tinnemans, Dinu Iuga

items.title: Sub-kJ/mol Precision at Practical Cost for Molecular Solids through Local Coupled Cluster Approaches
items.abstract: Generation of numerically converged coupled-cluster reference energies of molecular crystals remains highly non-routine.Yet, such data points are critically needed as computational methodologies strive to reach correlated wave-function accuracy in condensed-phase systems.Localized-orbital coupled-cluster approaches applied within
items.authors: Khanh Ngoc Pham, Marcin Modrzejewski, Péter R. Nagy, Jiří Klimeš

items.title: Phytochemical Analysis and evaluation of the Antioxidant Activity of Cissus microdonta Planch.
items.abstract: Cissus microdonta Planch. is traditionally used to treat jaundice in Madagascar. This study aimed to investigate the phytochemical profile of Cissus microdonta stems and evaluate its antioxidant activity. Hexane (1.75%), ethyl acetate (3.74%), and ethanol (1.67%) extracts of the plant stems were obtained by maceration. Phytochemical screening was performed. The antioxidant activity of the plant was evaluated using the DPPH assay. Compounds from the active extracts were isolated using liquid chromatography on silica gel and identified via spectroscopic analysis. The presence of alkaloids, leucoanthocyanins, saponins, triterpenes, saturated sterols, and leucoanthocyanidins was established. The evaluation of the antioxidant activity of the ethanolic extract of the plant revealed significant free-radical-scavenging capacity. One compound was isolated from the active ethyl acetate extract and identified as ursolic acid. This research has enhanced the understanding of the phytochemical profile and biological properties of Cissus microdonta Planch., suggesting that the plant may be a potential source of natural antioxidants.
items.authors: Séraphine Kanto Aricia OLIARISOA, Fanamperantsoa Andrianina RAMANAMIHAJA, Faramalala Louise RABEMANDROSO, Stanislas Fulgence LAHADSON, Herilala Léa RASOANAIVO

items.title: Structuring High-Entropy Oxides at the Nanoscale: Ordered Mesoporous (CrMnFeCoNi)Ox Thin Films for High-Performance Oxygen Evolution Reaction Catalysis
items.abstract: The synthesis of high-entropy oxides (HEOs) with nanoscale architectures is challenging, since both the peculiar crystalline structure with statistical element occupancy and the desired nanomorphology must be controlled. Here, ordered mesoporous (spinel) (CrMnFeCoNi)Ox HEO thin films were prepared via soft-templating and dip-coating under tailored synthesis conditions, and the influence of calcination temperature on their structural evolution and alkaline oxygen evolution reaction (OER) performance was investigated. Electron microscopy revealed a temperature-dependent development of an ordered mesoporous architecture with 15–20 nm pores using polyisobutylene-block-poly(ethylene oxide) (PIB-b-PEO) as structure-directing agent. Energy-dispersive spectroscopy and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy demonstrated a near-equiatomic, spatially homogeneous distribution of all transition metals at the surface and in the bulk. Transmission electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction revealed a temperature-induced transition from an amorphous to nanocrystalline cubic spinel structure at 600 °C. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicated a transformation from a high-valence, defective/hydroxylated surface composition rich in Cr6+, Mn3+, Co2+, and Ni2+ species at 300–400 °C to more low-valence surface states with increased lattice-oxygen contribution at 500–600 °C. The mesoporous HEO thin film annealed at 400 °C for 5 min exhibited one of the best OER performances ever reported (η10 = 273 mV at 10 mA cm−2 and Rct = 3.9 Ω at 1.5 V vs. RHE) in alkaline electrolyte. Overall, the structural evolution and OER performance of HEO thin films follow a temperature-dependent activity trend based on the balance and interplay of surface area, crystallinity, oxygen defects, and catalytically active species at the surface, highlighting the necessity of precise control of the synthesis conditions and formulation of structure-property relationships for improving the OER performance of compositionally complex catalysts.
items.authors: Qingyang Wu, Ann-Kristin Stief, Hikmet Sezen, Stefan Lauterbach, Barbara Gonzalez-Navarrete, Marc Widenmeyer

items.title: Spin states, electronic structure and phonon properties of ZnxFe[Fe(CN)6] (x = 0 – 1) by hybrid density functional theory
items.abstract: Hexacyanoferrates (HCF) or Prussian blue analogues (PBAs) have emerged as potent ion insertion materials for battery electrodes. They are also among the very few hosts in which reversible insertion of multivalent ions such as Zn 2+ into the framework is experimentally established. Zinc-containing ZnFe[Fe(CN) 6 ] members of the iron hexacyanoferrate series are particularly interesting for the anode-free zinc cells where cathode can supply the entire zinc inventory. Yet essentially nothing is fundamentally known about them. Here we report the symmetry, spin states, electronic structure and lattice dynamics of ZnFe[Fe(CN) 6 ], calculated within the all-electron linear combination of atomic orbitals (LCAO) approach using the hybrid B1WC exchange–correlation functional. We show by group-theoretical analysis that ordered occupation of a single interstitial 32 f site of the cubic Fm 3̄ m parent generates the observed rhombohedral R 3 m symmetry within the primitive cell, without recourse to a supercell, and that the resulting tetrahedral zinc coordination is consistent with the rhombohedral phases reported experimentally for Zn-containing hexacyanoferrates. By considering all site resolved spin state/configurations, we identify the low spin (LS) state on two Fe ions (i.e., Fe LS C +Fe LS N ) as the ground state in the rhombohedral ZnFe[Fe(CN) 6 ]. The first excited state is given by Fe LS C +Fe HS N and is separated by about 0.5 eV/f.u. from the ground state. We validated our calculation model by calculating the spin states/configurations in two reference materials, namely Fe[Fe(CN) 6 ] andKFe[Fe(CN) 6 ]. For KFe[Fe(CN) 6 ], the B1WC functional correctly reproduces the experimentally established configuration of LS state on the C-coordinated Fe and high spin (HS) state on the N-coordinated Fe. The dynamical stability of rhombohedral ZnFe[Fe(CN) 6 ] is confirmed by phonon calculations at the L, Γ, Z, and F points and by phonon dispersion curves along the L–Γ–Z path obtained using two supercell sizes. The calculated Raman spectrum for rhombohedral ZnFe[Fe(CN) 6 ] exhibits a pronounced gap of approx. 1400 cm −1 between the low and high frequency regions. The high frequency region of Raman spectrum is dominated by intense C–N stretching vibrations, whereas the low frequency region contains two well-resolved peaks due to bending vibration involving Fe N , N and C atoms and stretching motion of Fe N –N bond, respectively.
items.authors: Denis Gryaznov, Linas Vilčiauskas

items.title: Talking to instruments: device-integration standards for self-driving laboratories
items.abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are rapidly outgrowing the single-instrument prototype, scaling into multi-instrument and multi-site platforms that run autonomous discovery across chemistry, materials science, biotechnology, pharmaceutical re-search and adjacent domains. What now decides whether an SDL can scale, share its integrations and federate experiments is no longer the algorithms or the robots, but the software layer that orchestrates heterogeneous devices. Today that layer is the bottleneck: a fast-growing ecosystem of open-source orchestrators in which most have built device integration on their own bespoke conventions instead of adopting a formally governed standard. The result is predictable and costly. Integrations do not transfer between laboratories, orchestrators cannot interoperate and many new SDLs rebuild their device-control layer from scratch. Crucially, this is an engineering coordination problem, not a fundamental scientific one and therefore among the most tractable bottlenecks in autonomous science. We map the device-integration standards landscape onto the open-source orchestrator ecosystem, compare the leading options and give scenario-driven guidance on when to use each. We then translate the requirements of autonomous operation into a concrete deliverable: a set of testable engineering criteria and a weighted procurement scorecard that defines an autonomous-ready control interface and gives institutional buyers the leverage to demand it; these requirements do not change as orchestration turns agentic: whether an instrument is driven by a program or by a language-model agent through a model-facing protocol, it is only as safe and reliable as the interface it exposes. Adopted at scale, these requirements turn device integration from a burden repaid lab by lab into shared infrastructure,
items.authors: Willi Gottstein, Lukas Bromig, Matthias Arnold, Sina Barazandeh, Joseph S Brown, Keith A. Brown

items.title: Accelerated Langevin Dynamics Simulation via Neural Network-Driven Importance Sampling
items.abstract: Atomistic simulations are often restricted by timescale limitations when systems become trapped in metastable energy basins. The transitions between these metastable states are rare events and they dictate the long-term evolution of the system. We present an importance sampling framework to accelerate the time scale of Langevin dynamics simulations. The framework uses a neural network parameterized importance function to bias the dynamics, enhancing the efficiency of rare-transition sampling while preserving relative probabilities between transition paths. We provide a rigorous mathematical formulation to recover the original transition rates between metastable states from the biased dynamics, and use a branching random walk algorithm to control the statistical variance of the estimated rates. We validate the framework on 2- and 14-dimensional problems, as well as the system of 7 Lennard-Jones discs (d = 14) model. We further apply it to two realistic materials systems: the diffusion of a Pt adatom on the Pt(001) surface (d = 387) and the migration of a vacancy in BCC \alpha-iron (d = 2055). The framework provides a scalable foundation for accelerating the simulation of rare events in atomistic systems.
items.authors: Michael Kim, Wei Cai

items.title: Polymer Property Prediction via an Automated Molecular Dynamics Pipeline and Transfer Learning
items.abstract: For many existing and emerging applications, there is a great need to develop novel polymeric materials with highly tuned properties. In the quest to design materials from highly abundant natural resources or waste materials, there is a vast design space that has remained substantially unexplored. Machine learning approaches can help guide toward improved properties, but these approaches often suffer from a lack of high quality data, the acquisition of which can be tedious, time-consuming, and expensive. In silico atomistic simulations are a promising approach to generate data that are highly correlated to real polymer properties, but simulations of polymers present myriad challenges including accurate and automatic force field parameterization, initial configuration generation, and long relaxation times which make it extremely difficult to perform such simulations in a high-throughput manner. Here, we present a computational pipeline starting from SMILES strings of reactants to automatically generate force field parameters and initial system coordinates for subsequent molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of short oligomers that have much faster relaxation times than the corresponding polymer melts. Because most measurable properties of oligomeric fluids are not the same as those of the corresponding polymers of much higher degree of polymerization, and indeed many properties of polymer phases do not exist for such liquids, we employ a transfer learning scheme to predict polymer properties from the oligomer thermophysical data. Using this approach, we are able to achieve improved property predictions for a number of polymer properties, including gas permeabilities. These improvements are most dramatic when experimental data are sparse and when the experimental observables are most directly correlated to simulation properties.
items.authors: Jeffrey N. Law, Daria Lazarenko, Timotej Bernat, Brandon C. Knott, Michael R. Shirts

items.title: YB_Mol Studio: an agent-integrated visual editing platform for molecular and materials design
items.abstract: Molecular and materials design requires researchers to inspect structures, edit molecular objects and connect each change to computation. Artificial intelligence (AI) agents add another operating mode: they need executable molecular operations, visible intermediate states and a way to continue from prior results. Here we present YB_Mol Studio, an agent-integrated visual editing platform for molecular and materials design. Its molecular design core, yb_mol, represents atoms, bonds, coordinates, structural hierarchy and periodic information in editable molecular objects. Studio connects this core to direct visual editing, YB_Agent execution, a persistent Live workspace and local or remote scientific computation. Researchers can select and modify structures through the interface, inspect resulting states and continue a design manually or with the agent. YB_Agent can execute molecular operations through yb_mol, use specialist prediction or evaluation methods and publish results back into the same workspace. Molecular-object comparisons and operation benchmarks characterize the platform foundation, while three application workspaces exercise it on biomolecular and periodic-material workloads. YB_Mol Studio links human judgment, interactive visualization, agent execution and computational feedback in one continuing design environment.
items.authors: Yanbo Zhao, Shuai Zhang, Shenggang Li, Zezhong Miao, Haijiao Fu, Miaomiao Wang

items.title: TRMC and NEXAFS Reveal Fast Electron Transfer to Ce3+/Oxygen-Vacancy Traps in Non-Covalent CexOy/C3N4 Interface for Photocatalytic H2
items.abstract: Earth-abundant photocatalysts for solar H₂ struggle to absorb deep visible light and separate charges at the same time. Here we show that a small amount of reduced ceria on carbon nitride achieves both. Non covalent CexOy/C3N4 heterostructures with 4% and 7% cerium oxide were compared with CeO2 and C3N4 references for H₂ evolution at 410 and 465 nm. The key turns out to be not how much ceria is added, but in which state and how well it is spread. At 4%, ceria forms finely dispersed, oxygen-deficient nanoparticles rich in Ce3+/oxygen-vacancy (Ov) defects, as revealed by Ce M4,5- and O K-edge NEXAFS and supported by XPS, which shows reduced cerium, no fluorite lattice oxygen and the highest surface exposure of Ce. At 7%, the particles agglomerate. These defects extend light absorption into the visible range and act as electron traps: time-resolved microwave conductivity and photoluminescence reveal faster, productive electron transfer from C3N4 to ceria at 4%. As a result, the 4% composite delivers ~682 µmol g-1 h -1 (AQY ~0.57% at 410 nm), outperforming all other samples at both wavelengths. With a surface area similar to C3N4, the gain is electronic and defect-driven, not textural.
items.authors: Ingrid F. Silva, Heer Shah, Christian Kupfer, Asia Patriarchi, Erwan Paineau, Maria Rita Cicconi

items.title: Thioiminium Salt Catalyzed Chemoselective Late Stage Halogenation Using N-Halosuccinimides
items.abstract: C−H halogenation plays a central role in drug discovery. It enables rapid molecular diversification and provides a direct means to tune the metabolic and biological properties of drug candidates. However, selective halogenation of less reactive arenes remains challenging, particularly when aromatic and benzylic C−H bonds coexist in the same molecule. Here, we introduce a thioiminium salt-based Lewisbase catalyst that activates readily available N-halosuccinimides for selective aromatic and benzylic halogenation with complementary control. Notably, the method enables late-stage aromatic bromination of natural products, pharmaceuticals, peptides and heterocycles and can be extended to aromatic chlorination using N-chlorosuccinimide. The practicality of this method is demonstrated by four gramscale syntheses, catalyst recycling and post-synthetic diversification. Mechanistic and computational studies reveal distinct electrophilic and radical pathways, with the catalyst counter anion acting as a molecular switch for chemoselectivity between aromatic and benzylic bromination.
items.authors: Debasis Sahoo, Upasi Goswami, Haren Konwar, Arnab Mondal, Avijit Maiti, Tuhin Patra

items.title: Damage–repair kinetics and phase stiffness in a site-diluted XY model: implications for irradiated superconductors
items.abstract: Neutron damage lowers the transition temperature of REBCO conductors approximately linearly with displacement damage, and annealing recovers part of it, implicating phase stiffness. We model this competition as a two-dimensional XY lattice of the superconducting phase whose sites are damaged at a rate rising with local phase disorder and repaired stochastically, simulated by kinetic Monte Carlo. A mean-field reduction predicts bistability; the lattice shows no hysteresis or dependence on the initial state in the ranges tested (L ≤ 64) because the closure of the reduction fails. At zero field, symmetry-preserving repair restores spontaneous coherence and a twist-response stiffness (validated on clean and diluted lattices) above an apparent threshold in the repair-to-damage ratio, bracketed by finite-size scans (L ≤ 96) at ρ between 7.00 and 7.75 (ρ between 5.50 and 6.00 with neighbor-phase repair), against ρ ≈ 2.5 without feedback; the equilibrium formula underestimates the driven stiffness by up to 30%. Numerically, ρ controls the state ever better, as damage slows relative to phase relaxation. Finite-size analysis of random dilution estimates the stiffness loss at f ≈ 0.25 ± 0.01; clustered damage tolerates more. An illustrative effective mapping gives approximately ten model sites per dpa. The model is uncalibrated.
items.authors: Leon Sandler

items.title: Mapping Spatially Heterogeneous and History-Dependent Hydrogel Mechanics Using Fluid-Driven Cyclic Shear
items.abstract: Soft porous materials in biological environments, such as the extracellular matrix, are frequently subjected to dynamic stresses transmitted by fluid motion, yet their internal deformation fields and microstructural evolution under repeated loading remain elusive. Here, we impose oscillatory shear on agarose hydrogels without solid contact by embedding a millimeter-scale gel block in a microfluidic channel and applying oscillatory pressure-driven flow over its exposed surface. Tracking fluorescent particles immobilized in the gel reveals a heterogeneous response: displacement increases toward the gel-fluid interface, whereas shear strain and shear rate are concentrated near the anchored base. Under oscillatory flow of constant amplitude and frequency, freshly prepared gels deform progressively less over successive cycles, whereas gels rested for 1 h after gelation maintain a nearly constant deformation amplitude. This temporal response is consistent with bulk rheometry showing increasing storage and loss moduli only in fresh gels. Gels matured under cyclic shear deform less than gels matured at rest for the same duration and, as confocal imaging shows, develop aligned fiber bundles not seen in gels matured at rest. These results show that hydrodynamic loading modulates post-gelation network maturation. This study also establishes this contact-free approach as a platform for studying the mechanics of soft porous materials under flow-induced deformation.
items.authors: Pragya Kushwaha, Xuxiang Qian, Sangwoo Shin, Xin Yong

items.title: Adaptation of a retrosynthetic tool to project-specific chemistry: oligomer synthesis case study
items.abstract: Retrosynthetic planning for discrete oligomers presents challenges that differ from those encountered for conventional small molecules because their synthesis often relies on repeated transformations applied at multiple related sites within a multistep route. In conventional template-based search, each application of a single-center reaction rule is represented as an independent action, causing repeated chemistry to consume additional search depth and potentially generating order-equivalent trajectories. Here, we showcase the adaptation of the SynPlanner retrosynthetic platform to oligomeric chemistry through the introduction of project-specific priority rules and a newly implemented Rule Multi-Application (RMA) mechanism. RMA enables repeated applications of the same single-center rule to be represented within a single search expansion, with the multiplicity determined dynamically from the molecular structure. Composite rules were additionally used to provide sequence-level guidance for selected ordered transformations. The approach was evaluated on two literature-derived targets: a linear oligoacetylacetone-derived oligomer and a macrocyclic calix[3]pyrrole. For the linear target, baseline planning generated 161 complete routes across 20 strategic-bond-pattern (SBP) clusters but did not reproduce the literature strategy. Combining priority-rule guidance, RMA, and sequence-level abstraction enabled exact recovery of the reported pathway. For the macrocyclic target, baseline planning failed to identify a complete route even after increasing the search budget to 10,000 iterations, whereas the RMA-enabled guided configuration generated 65 complete routes across three SBP clusters, including routes reproducing the strategic-bond pattern of the literature synthesis. These results demonstrate that adapting a retrosynthetic planner to oligomeric chemistry requires not only access to relevant reaction knowledge but also an appropriate representation of repeated transformations during multistep search.
items.authors: Almaz Gilmullin, Tagir Akhmetshin, Olga Klimchuk, Dragos Horvath, Timur Madzhidov, Yuki Ide

items.title: Engineering Bacteria and Their Vesicles for Therapy: Integrating Native Functions, Genetic Control, and Chemical Biology
items.abstract: Bacteria possess native capabilities that are difficult to reproduce using conventional therapeutic platforms, including active motility, environmental adaptation, localized proliferation, metabolite production, immune stimulation, and interactions with host-associated microbial communities. However, bacterial therapeutics are frequently organized either by microbial species or by engineering technology, obscuring how chassis selection, functional modification, and clinical application should be coordinated. This review presents a chassis-first framework for the development of bacterial therapeutics. We define the functional requirements associated with cancer, intestinal inflammation, metabolic disorders, infectious diseases, and vaccination, and classify therapeutic bacteria into established chassis, microbiome-derived chassis, and function-driven unconventional chassis. We then examine two complementary engineering routes. Genetic engineering enables attenuation, disease-responsive sensing, therapeutic-payload production, controlled release, and biological containment, whereas chemical biology–enabled biohybrid engineering introduces targeting, protection, catalytic activity, and external control through surface functionalization, bacteria-mediated biosynthesis and biomineralization, and whole-cell coating. Because living bacteria retain risks associated with replication, dissemination, and evolutionary instability, we further discuss therapeutic termination strategies and compare whole-cell systems with nonreplicating outer membrane vesicles and related membrane-based platforms. Finally, we examine the clinical translation of bacterial medicines in terms of administration route, biodistribution, pharmacodynamics, manufacturing, safety, and regulatory control. Collectively, this review proposes that bacterial therapeutics should be designed within an integrated framework linking native chassis phenotype, engineering module, and clinical scenario, thereby shifting the field from opportunistic strain modification toward function-guided and translationally tractable therapeutic design.
items.authors: Lihao Ji, Haomiao Huang, Yuhan Zhang, Tianqi Jiang, Zipeng Chen, Xiuxiu Wang

items.title: Pore-network homogeneity for mechanically reliable powder-compacted solid-electrolyte separators
items.abstract: All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) with alloy anodes require solid-electrolyte (SE) separators that sustain ion transport while accommodating repeated electrode-derived mechanical loads. However, the mechanical state of powder-compacted separators is commonly inferred from bulk porosity, averaged mechanical properties, or cell-level stack pressure changes, obscuring spatially heterogeneous local responses. Here, we show that pore-network homogeneity is a key determinant of the mechanical reliability of sulfide solid-electrolyte separators by governing local mechanical heterogeneity and stress localization. FIB-SEM tomography and spatially resolved nanoindentation reveal that a highly densified separator with a broad particle-size distribution (PSD) retains clustered pore-rich and mechanically compliant regions, whereas a narrower-PSD separator exhibits a more homogeneous pore network and local mechanical response. Despite comparable cell-level pressure evolution, the two separators show markedly different cycling stability. Post-cycling microscopy reveals cracking and interfacial delamination in the heterogeneous separator, while microstructure-resolved simulations reveal stronger local stress amplification consistent with these observations. Controlled digital structures with identical D50 and porosity further isolate PSD-dependent changes in pore architecture and stress distribution. These findings establish pore-network homogeneity as a key design criterion for mechanically reliable solid-electrolyte separators beyond ionic conductivity and bulk densification.
items.authors: Hyeok-Rae Cho, Hyeong-Jong Kim, Jae-Seung Kim, Beom Jin Park, Youngkyung Kim, Daeyeon Lee

items.title: Exact orientational thermodynamics of multipole rank pairs: a two-valued low-temperature heat-capacity law, with new data for 28 rank pairs (L = 2-24) and 29 real molecule pairs
items.abstract: New results and new data reported in this work. This paper reports a primary data set and the law it yields, not a survey of the literature. (i) Orientational partition functions 𝑍(𝑦) and low-temperature interaction heat capacities 𝛾 = 𝐶𝑣/𝑘𝐵 are computed for 28 multipole rank pairs spanning 𝐿 = 𝑛 +𝑚 = 2 to 𝐿 = 24, each entry obtained by up to three mutually independent numerical routes — the large-𝑦 tail of the thermal coupling function, the exact fluctuation formula, and the sublevel-volume exponent — and each with the coupling-minimum structure measured independently of the exponent. (ii) The exact second-moment identity is verified by direct quadrature for nine rank pairs to a maximum relative deviation of 6.8 × 10−14. (iii) Zero-parameter predictions — dominant channel, coupling scale and freezing temperature 𝑇∗ — are given for 29 real molecule pairs (H2O, NH3, CO2, C2H4, CH4, BF3, CH3I, SF6, among others), and split them into the two low-temperature classes. (iv) A negative result is reported rather than omitted: the widely used singleparameter universality of the thermal coupling function Φ𝑛𝑚(𝑦) is falsified, with relative deviations up to 47%. (v) The orientation average is reduced exactly to a three-dimensional integral and the kernel is obtained from a three-term recurrence valid at any rank, which removes the monomial-expansion ceiling of the earlier 𝐿 ≤ 16 version. Every number quoted is tabulated in the main text (Tables 1, 2, 2a-2c, 3, 4) and in the Supporting Information (S1-S12), and the complete machine-readable data and code are openly archived (Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23086356).
items.authors: Fuxing Lin

items.title: Tension-Limited Leaflet-Asymmetry Budding Predicts the Size and Rate of Tumour Ectosome Shedding
items.abstract: In fatty-acid protocells, growth by outer-leaflet monomer uptake generates a transbilayer area imbalance that is relieved by shedding nano-vesicles once the reduced imbalance ∆a exceeds a critical value ∆ac = O(1), as described by area-difference elasticity (ADE). It is tempting to read modern tumour ectosome shedding as the same physics. We show that the naive transfer fails, and derive the version that does not. A protocell is tensionless; the plasma membrane of a cancer cell is not, and its apparent tension (σ ∼ 10−5–10−4 N m−1) imposes an area cost that is absent from the protocell treatment. Replacing the shape-instability criterion with an explicit energy balance for bud formation, we obtain a budding threshold in the differential leaflet tension, ∆τc = √ 8κσ/h, and a parameter-free bud radius at threshold, r∗ = √ 2κ/σ,
items.authors: Peter Mikuláš

items.title: How does spatio-temporal optimisation affect the siting and operation of direct air capture systems?
items.abstract: The climate crisis is driving the urgent development of negative emission technologies, such as adsorption-based direct air capture (DAC). Although DAC holds promise, it remains costly and requires further technological innovation, design optimisation, and supply chain development to scale effectively and achieve meaningful climate impact. DAC performance is influenced by both local ambient (e.g., temperature, humidity) and energy conditions (e.g., upstream emissions, costs). Previous studies have typically evaluated DAC systems under constant ambient and energy conditions, used static models that do not provide temporally resolved results, or restricted their analysis to limited case studies. These restrictions may lead to an incomplete assessment of DAC performance and suboptimal decision-making. This study presents the dynamic DAC + energy supply (DACES) optimisation framework, which explicitly accounts for spatial and temporal variations in ambient and energy conditions, and demonstrates its application to the province of Alberta, Canada using highresolution data from 2024. The DACES model can address two essential questions without reverting to static modelling or time-averaged input assumptions: (i) which locations are better suited for DAC deployment than others and (ii) how DAC should be operated. Coupled with a genetic algorithm that minimises net carbon capture costs, the DACES model answers these questions while maintaining computational tractability. The results demonstrate that spatio-temporal optimisation—through the selection of more favourable DAC locations combined with adaptive cycle designs—reduces estimated costs by up to 20 %. Specifically, the use of dynamic conditions in the decision-making process favours the positioning of DAC systems in northern Alberta, whereas constant conditions would have placed them several hundred kilometres further south. An analysis of 32 external conditions across different stages of the cycle identified ambient temperature at the start of adsorption, relative humidity at the end of adsorption, and upstream emissions and costs at the start of desorption as the parameters most influential to cycle performance. Results further show that, for optimal cycle designs, the system should (i) align cycle design with the minima of these parameters at their respective stages, since they determine the extent of pre-desorption conditions and the associated costs of net removal during desorption; and (ii) introduce strategically timed waiting periods between DAC phases to align operation with external conditions, trading DAC productivity for reduced regeneration energy. Overall, the findings highlight that accounting for spatio-temporal variability and optimising cycle design at the individual-cycle level can considerably enhance DAC performance and reduce operational costs.
items.authors: Malte Glaser, Sean T. McCoy

items.title: Metal/Support Interfaces Overcome Reactivity Constraints of the Oxygen Reduction Reaction
items.abstract: Oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) catalysts are limited by precious metal costs and reactivity limitations by bond order conservation. We establish a conceptual framework to explain how low-dimensional Pt, Au, and Ag films on low-cost carbide/nitride supports transcend these limitations. Electronegativity differences between metal films and support terminations govern interfacial charge transfer, producing ligand effects that stabilize metal films, and raise the maximum of the ORR volcano plot. These ligand effects are intuitively rationalized and codified into a reactivity descriptor for ORR intermediates at metal/support interfaces. This descriptor combines conventional d-band properties with interfacial charge transfer, metal-support bond order, and strain. This study shortlists 19 stable catalysts with superior ORR reactivity relative to Pt (111), including Au-based catalysts that are inactive in unsupported forms. This work provides a new perspective for understanding and predicting ORR reactivity at metal/support interfaces, while expanding the ORR catalyst design space.
items.authors: Asmee M. Prabhu, Arravind Subramanian, Kah-Meng Yam, Bryan C. S. Lee, Neeru Chaudhary, Lavie Rekhi

items.title: Chemical Non-Innocence in Mn Porphyrin-Catalyzed Nitrene Transfer
items.abstract: Manganese porphyrins have been widely employed as catalysts for nitrogen-group transfer (NGT) and oxygen-atom transfer (OAT) reactions with olefins and C–H bonds. These transformations are typically proposed to proceed via high-valent manganese nitrenoid and oxo intermediates, respectively. While porphyrin redox non-innocence — in which electron transfer from the ligand to the metal delocalizes high-valent states across the metal and the ancillary ligand — is well established. The potential role of porphyrin chemical non-innocence — in which an atom or group inserts into the M–pyrrolide bond — is much less appreciated. Here, we demonstrate that treatment of Mn(tpp)Cl with iminoiodinanes (PhI═NR, R = Ts (tosyl) and Ns (nosyl)) affords the corresponding tucked-in Mn porphyrins in which the iminoiodinane-derived nitrene fragment has inserted into one of the Mn–N bonds. Nitrene insertion into the Mn–N bond was characterized by NMR, UV-vis, and high-frequency and -field EPR (HFEPR) spectroscopies, as well as single-crystal X-ray diffraction. Nitrene insertion into the Mn–N bond is reversible under both thermal and photochemical conditions; untucking in the presence of styrene affords the corresponding aziridine, demonstrating that the tucked-in porphyrin can function as a latent nitrene equivalent. In situ UV-vis spectroscopy and kinetics experiments of Mn(tpp)Cl-catalyzed styrene aziridination demonstrate that, despite the chemical viability of nitrene insertion / de-insertion reactions, the formation of tuck-in porphyrins is slow relative to olefin aziridination. These results demonstrate that reversible formation of nitrene tuck-in porphyrins is chemically accessible and represents a latent source of electrophilic nitrene equivalents and that in the context of Mncatalyzed aziridination, these elementary steps are slow relative to catalysis.
items.authors: Arka Sinha, Ryan X. Gruen, Matthew T. Figgins, Joseph Reibenspies, Joshua Telser, J. Krzystek

items.title: Single and Multiexciton Dynamics in Porphyrin Nanorings
items.abstract: Exciton transport in molecular assemblies is typically studied in linear chains and polydisperse aggregates, where chain ends perturb the electronic structure and structural inhomogeneity can obscure size-dependent trends. Molecular nanorings overcome both limitations: they are end-group-free macrocycles with well-defined sizes, while their dimensions can be synthetically tuned from a few to several tens of porphyrin units. Here, we use intensity-cycled femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy to disentangle single- and multiexciton dynamics in a series of fully conjugated molecular nanorings containing 6–40 Zn-porphyrin units. By isolating the third-, fifth-, and seventh-order nonlinear responses, we independently track single-, two-, and three-exciton dynamics, enabling the ring-size dependence of exciton–exciton annihilation (EEA) to be determined without relying on a priori kinetic assumptions. The EEA rate decreases systematically with increasing ring size, accompanied by a crossover from annihilation-limited to diffusion-limited EEA between 20 and 30 porphyrin units. The smallest nanoring exhibits no resolvable multiexciton dynamics, consistent with exciton delocalisation across the entire ring or equivalent sub-instrument response EEA, whereas larger rings exhibit increasingly diffusive exciton motion as static disorder limits delocalisation. The retrieved exciton diffusion coefficients are two to three orders of magnitude higher than those we previously reported, indicating that the assumptions inherent to conventional intensity-dependent fitting can substantially underestimate exciton mobility.
items.authors: Erico M. Braun, Michael Jirasek, Harry L. Anderson, Stephen R. Meech, Ismael A. Heisler, Giovanni Bressan

items.title: Chilean Papaya Bioprospecting for Human α-Glucosidase: Near-Native Pose Recovery in CtMGAM Docking
items.abstract: Chilean papaya phytochemistry motivates examination of a defined natural-product panel in the context of human intestinal alpha-glucosidases. Before docking can justify molecular prioritization, the procedure must show that it both generates relevant conformations and selects them reliably. The present study evaluated this evidence at the C-terminal catalytic subunit of human maltase-glucoamylase (CtMGAM), using complete native acarbose as a redocking benchmark for seven Vina/Vinardo protocols at two crystallographic copies. Separate analyses assessed a carbohydrate-docking workflow across enzyme families and the structural suitability of deposited ligand copies. Across the complete CtMGAM matrix, near-native acarbose poses were accessible within the first three emitted modes at both copies; consistent first-rank recovery, however, occurred at only one of the two copies. Short-list recovery therefore did not establish reliable automated selection across the two copies. The cross-family workflow showed limited recovery among eligible poses, while exact-copy screening identified density and catalytic-site context as constraints on benchmark choice. Together, these results define an evidence boundary for interpreting docking in Chilean papaya bioprospecting: the natural-product panel is chemically defined but cannot yet be ranked by the evaluated procedures. Direct biochemical assays are required to establish its activity at CtMGAM.
items.authors: Roberto Pizarro Díaz

items.title: Exact concentration regions for stimulus-switched competitive binding under finite depletion
items.abstract: The reported C/B composition of a published pH-programmed coordination cage provides a stringent test for transferring binary binding constants into a competitive mixture. At pH 7.5, the observed C/B ratio requires Keff B (7.5) 6.38885 M−1, but the entire quoted marginal rectangle for the transferred B affinities lies above this bound under the same-site model and fixed reported pKa. This tension motivates a bounded inverse calculation for finite-depletion competitive binding. Starting from the established one-site equilibrium model, target odds factor as OaOb = S∆, separating the controlled-free-concentration selectivity swing from finite-depletion effects. For two guests with one total fixed, monotonicity converts independent fidelity and occupancy requirements into explicit one-sided concentration thresholds whose intersection is the complete admissible interval. A pairwise endpoint bound gives a necessary consistency test for observed ratios in mixtures containing additional same-site competitors. The construction is extended to two independently variable totals through exact boundary curves parameterized by free-host concentration, without assuming convexity or a one-interval topology. In the Cullen system, the binary C/B projection shows that finite depletion changes a 95% decision, while a full acid/C/B map independently underpredicts middle-pH C dominance under transferred constants. A second application to a pH-responsive naphthotube shows the high-selectivity-margin regime: depletion changes the maximin by only 0.23 percentage points and the 95% window remains broad. The method provides model-conditional concentration windows, concentration-region maps and parameter-transfer consistency tests.
items.authors: Hyun Seo

items.title: Large language models as collaborators in molecular thermodynamics: a case study of the LLM-assisted development of SAFT-VR IMP, an equation of state for polar fluids
items.abstract: Whether large language models (LLMs) can contribute to non-trivial science, beyond summarising literature and writing routine code, is an open question. We report a case study in which an LLM (Claude) was asked to formulate, implement, verify and parameterise a new equation of state of the statistical associating fluid theory (SAFT) family. The target was a SAFT-VR variant for polar and dipolar molecules in which the segments interact through the isotropic multipolar potential (IMP) of Müller and Gelb, expressed as a temperature-dependent sum of Sutherland terms and treated with the Barker–Henderson perturbation theory of SAFT-VR Mie and SAFT-VR Sum. Over three sessions the LLM produced a stepby-step derivation, a 600-line implementation in the open-source Julia package Clapeyron.jl, a suite of 97 verification tests, a parameter-estimation pipeline applied to DIPPR data for six cyclic ethers, ketones and a sulfide, and a comparison with the group-contribution SAFT-γ
items.authors: Werner A. Müller, Benoit Creton, Carlos Nieto-Draghi, Erich A. Müller

items.title: Adsorption and Separation of Dihydroxybenzenes by Colorimetric Molecular Adsorbing Host•Guest Crystals
items.abstract: Hydrogen-bonded Organic Frameworks (HOFs) form a rapidly expanding alternative to Metal Organic Frameworks (MOFs). Among HOFs, the Molecular Adsorbing Host•Guest ( MAHG ) crystals introduced here combine cucurbit[8]uril (CB[8]) macrocycles and a tetraacid derivative of diphenyl-viologen (TETRAC). Despite their non-porous crystalline framework, MAHG crystals enable the diffusion of dihydroxybenzenes (DHB), which tend to localize in specific crystalline sites. The diffusion of DHB inside the permeable crystals is followed by striking color changes related to the formation of charge-transfer (CT) complexes between the electron-rich DHB and the electron-poor viologen units confined within the CB[8] cavities. Kinetic and crystallographic studies indicate the possible separation of DHB mixtures. This work highlights the potential of MAHG crystals for the rapid detection of DHB via colorimetric changes and their separation in water, offering a promising approach for industrial applications dedicated to hydroquinone and catechol production.
items.authors: Melvin Raulin, Eric Merlet, Florian Ferrer, Isabelle Braccini, Didier Siri, Brice Kauffmann

items.title: From Retrosynthetic Prediction to the Bench: Experimental Evaluation of Computer-Generated Synthetic Routes
items.abstract: Retrosynthesis tools propose bond disconnections and precursor assignments, but the chemist must still evaluate these choices and select reaction conditions and purification before a route can be run. In this work, we examine 53 PostEra Manifold and AiZynthFinder proposals for three small organic targets by combining chemist assessments with selected synthesis outcomes. Proposals were rejected or deprioritised for different reasons: incorrect connectivity, unsupported transformations, or extra steps and costly precursors in routes that would otherwise work. For a methoxy-substituted biaryl ketone, a Suzuki–Miyaura coupling using the chemist-preferred assignment of coupling partners gave 94% isolated yield. For a naphthylphenol, coupling with 2hydroxyphenylboronic acid gave 92% isolated yield with an aryl bromide and 7% with the corresponding chloride under the same procedure. The chloride result supports the chemist’s preference for the bromide, whereas the 92% yield shows that the earlier concern about this boronic acid, based on its behaviour in water, was not limiting under the tested conditions. We therefore propose that each generated route be judged on four separate points: whether it gives the correct target, whether the transformation is chemically supported, whether the route is practical, and whether it has been tested experimentally.
items.authors: Laura d’Andrea, Heidi Fuglsang Christiansen, Casper Steinmann

items.title: Inconsistent odor-threshold measurements limit prediction from molecular structure
items.abstract: Existing work treats odor detection threshold prediction as a supervised regression problem, assuming published thresholds are clean targets. In current public datasets, they are not: values come from different measurement sources and often disagree for the same molecule. Across the three largest public air-phase compilations, thresholds for identical molecules differ systematically by median factors of 3 to 11. Individual source studies vary around a compound’s underlying threshold by about 1.4 log 10 units, so under an independent-source approximation, a new study is expected to differ from the compiled value by about 1.6 log 10 units. This exceeds the best structure-based model’s error against that value (root-mean-square error 1.34), meaning the model matches the published compilation more closely than a new experiment would be expected to. Although averaging multiple studies makes the compiled value more precise, its remaining uncertainty still accounts for at least one-third of the model’s prediction-error variance, and a single source-study threshold has estimated reliability near 0.5. Changing the molecular representation, by comparison, changes root-mean-square error by only about 0.2 log 10 units. We therefore introduce a joint calibration model that places the compilations on a common scale, estimates source-specific offsets and noise, and improves cross-compilation prediction over a simple fixed-offset correction while providing calibrated uncertainty. These results show that progress in odor detection threshold prediction depends not only on better molecular models, but also on better measurements and methods that account for disagreement across data sources.
items.authors: Anand R. Mysorekar, Lekha Challappa

items.title: Self-quenched growth of monodisperse SnO2 nanocrystals—insensitive to synthesis conditions
items.abstract: Metal oxide thin film fabrication from colloidal nanocrystal dispersions separates the materials synthesis from the device (layer) fabrication, enabling fast solution processing. However, nanocrystal ink syntheses can be still too complex to be truly scalable for large-area ultra-lowcost applications such as solar modules. Here, we present a self-quenched (by precipitation) nanocrystal synthesis at room temperature. The synthesis is independent of the precursor concentrations, precursor addition speed (injection vs. slow addition), mixing dynamics of the solutions, reaction duration, and temperature. Crystalline and monodisperse tin(IV) oxide nanocrystals ( 3 nm diameter) are obtained with a near-unity reaction yield. After purification, the nanocrystal surface is modified with acetate ligands and brought into a colloidal dispersion, again with near-unity yield. Nip perovskite solar cells containing tin oxide nanocrystal thin films 2 achieve power conversion efficiencies of at least 21%. This method introduces a highly scalable SnO2 nanocrystal ink synthesis, which may be applicable to other metal oxides for coating technologies such as displays, windows, and perovskite solar modules, as well as the deposition on polymer films.
items.authors: Yongli Lu, Meng-Chen Shih, Shaun Tan, Yu-Kuan Lin, Moungi Bawendi, Matthias J. Grotevent
items.title_zh: 自熄生长的单分散SnO2纳米晶体——对合成条件不敏感
items.summary_zh: 金属氧化物薄膜的制备通过胶体纳米晶体分散液将材料合成与器件（层）制造分离，从而实现快速溶液处理。然而，纳米晶体墨水的合成仍然过于复杂，难以真正实现大面积超低成本应用，如太阳能模块。本文提出了一种在室温下自熄（通过沉淀）纳米晶体合成的方法。该合成与前驱体浓度、前驱体添加速度（注入与缓慢添加）、溶液混合动力学、反应时间和温度无关。获得了晶体和单分散的四氧化锡纳米晶体（直径约3纳米），反应产率接近100%。经过纯化后，纳米晶体表面被乙酸配体修饰，并再次以接近100%的产率形成胶体分散液。含有锡氧化物纳米晶体薄膜的钙钛矿太阳能电池实现了至少21%的光电转换效率。该方法引入了一种高度可扩展的SnO2纳米晶体墨水合成，可能适用于其他金属氧化物的涂层技术，如显示器、窗户和钙钛矿太阳能模块，以及在聚合物薄膜上的沉积。

items.title: Spatially Refined Analysis of Emission Burdens and Equity from Light-, Medium-, and Heavy-Duty Vehicle Traffic in the United States
items.abstract: We estimate block-level emission intensities of nitrogen oxides (NO X ) and fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) from on-road vehicle traffic for every census block in the United States, combining MOVES-based emission factors with street level traffic data. We use this spatially refined, computationally efficient, and policy-sensitive metric to evaluate emissions burden. Despite comprising less than 11% of vehicle kilometers traveled, we find that medium- and heavy-duty trucks account for 46% of NO X and 50% of PM 2.5 emission burden nationally — with PM 2.5 burden from trucks dominated by exhaust emissions while tire and brake wear constitute nearly half of light-duty vehicle PM 2.5 burden. People of color face emission burdens averaging 40% above the national mean, with Asian populations exceeding 60%, and lower-income populations face 20–25% higher burdens. Statistically significant racial-ethnic or income disparities are present in 85–89% of US counties. Critically, these disparities are not confined to large metropolitan areas. They are widespread across both urban and rural counties nationwide. We also show that spatial aggregation substantially attenuates estimated disparities of burdened groups, underscoring the importance of spatially refined analysis.
items.authors: Brittany Antonczak, Clare Nelson, Tammy Thompson, Mindi DePaola, Gregory Rowangould

items.title: Electronic and Steric Effects on the Photoswitching and Thermal Relaxation of Ortho-Substituted Pyrazole Azo Phthalimides
items.abstract: A series of ortho-substituted phthalimide–azopyrazole photoswitches bearing CH3, CF3, tert-Bu, and Ph groups was developed to determine how local steric and electronic perturbations control photochemical addressability and thermal Z→E relaxation. The substituents strongly altered the preferred irradiation wavelength while producing modest differences in the attainable Z-rich photostationary states. The CF3 derivative underwent E→Z photoisomerization at 530 nm, whereas the other derivatives were switched at 370 nm. TD-DFT analysis attributes this spectral differentiation to orbital reordering, configuration mixing, and redistribution of oscillator strength within the low-energy excited-state manifold. Thermal Z→E half-lives span more than three orders of magnitude, from 112 s for the CH3 derivative to 73 h for the CF3 derivative. Eyring analysis reveals predominantly entropic differentiation among the CH3, tert-Bu, and Ph derivatives, whereas CF3 persistence is primarily enthalpic. Adiabatic S0 calculations reproduce the experimental stability order but do not account for the substantially negative experimental activation entropies. Relaxed T1 scans and optimized S0/T1 crossing points identify accessible twisted crossing regions. The combined results support a multidimensional relaxation landscape in which CNNC torsion, azo-nitrogen bending, and changes in N=N bond character constitute coupled coordinates whose energetic and configurational accessibility is reshaped by ortho substitution.
items.authors: Sheelbhadra Chatterjee, Kosuke Nakashima, Miroslav Dangalov, Yasuyuki Matsushima, Shin-ichi Hirashima, Tsuyoshi Miura

items.title: Nucleotide-mediated catalytic peptide synthesis from aminonitriles
items.abstract: Aminonitriles are accessible from simple feedstock compounds and their hydrolysis offers an abiotic route to life’s amino acids on the early earth. However, controlled aqueous polymerisation of amino acids into peptides remains challenging. Here we show that peptides can be directly generated and elongated by aminonitriles when the latter are coupled to nucleotides as a phosphoramidate. Upon thiol catalysis and pH shifts, a series of selective reactivities drives iterative peptide bond formation in water. The high energy nitrile bond of aminonitriles circumvents amino acids’ need for concurrent activation chemistry in peptide elongation. Coupling the building blocks of life’s central biopolymers in this manner provides a pathway for early integration of peptides into biology.
items.authors: Luis Ohlendorf, Jyoti Singh, Erica Park, Sofija Spric, Qian Zhang, Josh Maiklem

items.title: Beyond Organic Molecules: MetalLipoDB, a Lipophilicity Dataset for Metal Complexes and Machine Learning Benchmarks
items.abstract: Lipophilicity governs the uptake, distribution and toxicity of drug candidates, yet the experimental logP datasets used to build predictive models contain almost exclusively organic molecules. Here we present MetalLipoDB, a manually curated dataset of 5158 experimental logP and logD values of complexes of 23 metals from 1192 articles, including 556 entries for multinuclear and heterometallic complexes, annotated with the measurement conditions and counterions. The dataset quantifies the inter-study reproducibility of these measurements (0.56 log units) and serves as a benchmark for machine learning, with a mean absolute error of 0.72–0.75 for complexes from unseen articles. For articles with at least four measurements, anchoring the predictions to three measured complexes of the series reduced the error on the remaining complexes from 0.73 to 0.51. MetalLipoDB, the code and an interactive web application (https://biometaldb.streamlit.app/) are openly available to support the design of metal-based drugs.
items.authors: Lev Krasnov, Dmitriy Malikov, Marina A. Kiseleva, Artem Lvov, Sergei V. Tatarin, Stanislav I. Bezzubov

items.title: AI Agents for CRISPR Diagnostics: From Automation to Bounded Autonomy
items.abstract: Recent years have witnessed rapid advances in clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) diagnostics, artificial intelligence (AI), and self-driving laboratories for automation. CRISPR diagnostics have emerged as a promising strategy for earlier disease detection, with Cas12a and Cas13a targeting DNA and RNA, respectively, and converting that recognition into collateral reporter cleavage. In parallel, different subsets of AI have advanced rapidly, with machine learning (ML) interpreting biosensor readouts, and large language models (LLMs) and AI agents applied to automation. Laboratory automation and self-driving platforms reduce the workload of human experimentalists and enable scale-up, having run long unattended campaigns in materials discovery. However, how these advances in AI, CRISPR diagnostics and automation could be integrated to enable a future of autonomous biosensing remains unresolved. In this perspective, we evaluate CRISPR diagnostics as autonomous systems, where analytical metrics alone cannot ensure robustness, failure-mode predictability, recoverability and auditability. We then propose a bounded-autonomy layer in which multimodal evidence, scored by ML, gates a Sense, quality control (QC), Decide, Act and Report loop, with guardrailed LLM agents invoked only when QC flags a run, selecting pre-validated actions under deterministic validation. By tying detectable failure modes to validated recovery actions, we outline a path toward bounded autonomy in CRISPR diagnostics, where a device unable to act safely abstains and escalates.
items.authors: Sina Jamalzadegan, Mahsa Bagi, Sepehr Soltani, Zahra Joudaki, Akhil Penumudy, David Haussler

items.title: Synthesis of nitride materials by atmospheric pressure metathesis
items.abstract: Nitride materials have many important technological applications, yet they remain underexplored compared to other classes of compounds, as reflected by the smaller number of reports in databases and literature. The primary reason for this is the difficulty of synthesizing nitrides, which must outcompete energetically stable molecular N 2 and oxide compounds. As a result, bulk synthesis of nitrides often requires high pressure or corrosive fluxes in addition to oxygen-free conditions. We present our perspective on the metathesis technique as an accessible method for synthesizing nitrides at or below atmospheric pressure for the broader chemistry community. To highlight the advantages of this synthesis approach, we also review traditional methods for bulk nitride synthesis, including high pressure techniques, sodium and halide fluxes, and gas- and liquid-ammonia-based routes. We provide a brief tutorial on metathesis reactions including tips and tricks to help researchers get started. Finally, we discuss the future outlook for metathesis reactions, with an opportunity for precise structural selection during nitride synthesis through the controlled formation of stable and metastable polymorphs within the multidimensional potential-energy landscape of material nucleation and growth.
items.authors: Anna Berseneva, Christopher Rom, Rebecca Smaha, Andriy Zakutayev

items.title: The Problem of NMR Data Analysis in Synthetic Chemistry: Why Is It Important to Understand Spectra?
items.abstract: High-resolution NMR (nuclear magnetic resonance) is one of the key methods for establishing the structures of organic compounds. Modern instrumentation and reference data provide a sufficient range of experiments for unambiguous assignment. However, in practice these resources are applied selectively. An assignment is commonly treated as complete once it no longer contradicts the expected structure. It is complete only when the spectrum as a whole has been explained, including signals at odds with that structure. The discussion is built on six papers retracted between 2020 and 2025, in which the reported structure was incorrect and the original assignment rested on NMR data. These cases are not used to estimate how often such errors occur, but to illustrate types of error that keep recurring in the literature. The same errors are then shown in a paper where the structure is correct and firmly supported by orthogonal methods. Two criteria are proposed for assessing a reported spectrum without access to the raw data. The first is the resolution indicated by the multiplet of the residual solvent signal. Therefore, this multiplet should remain visible in spectra reproduced in the Supporting Information. The second is the internal consistency of the reported data. The stated multiplicity must match the number of coupling constants. The notation must also make sense for the structure: simple descriptions such as “d” or “t” are not valid, for example, for the signals of a monosubstituted or unsymmetrically 1,4-disubstituted benzene ring. Automated approaches inherit rather than remove this difficulty: their output is accepted with the same confidence.
items.authors: Artur V. Eshtukov-Shcheglov

items.title: A New Route to Macrobicyclic Dibridgehead Diphopsphines P((CH 2 ) n ) 3 P; Reductive Demetalation of Cage-Like Fe(CO) 3 Adducts
items.abstract: When THF solutions of cage-like trans-Fe(CO) 3 (P((CH 2 ) n ) 3 P) ( 1 , n = a /10, b /12, c /14, d /16, e /18) are exposed to a potassium mirror, reduction occurs to give ferrate salts of the formula 2K + [(R 3 P)(CO) 3 Fe] 2– , as supported by IR data. Following additions of excess CO and methanol, the dibridgehead diphosphines P((CH 2 ) n ) 3 P ( 1a-e ) are isolated as white solids in 61-98% yields (average 80%) as mixtures of in/in and out/out isomers that interconvert by homeomorphic isomerization. This protocol represents an alternative to a photochemical demetalation that requires PMe 3 , as well as oxidative recipes that give dibridgehead diphosphine dioxides 1a-e ·2O with byproducts that are difficult to remove. The practicality of the new route is demonstrated by a half gram-scale synthesis of 1b .
items.authors: Simon M. Popovic, John A. Gladysz

items.title: Giant barocaloric effect from spin crossover in a green nitroprusside framework†
items.abstract: The interest in spin crossover for solid-state cooling is growing. We investigate the spin crossover transitions of [Fe(pyridine)2Fe(CN)5NO] and [Fe(pyrazine)Fe(CN)5NO] by single-crystal X-ray diffraction, high-pressure X-ray diffraction, magnetometry, and high-pressure calorimetry. The dehydrated form of the latter compound shows a reversible cooling effect (∆Tad,rev) of ∼15K at 1.2 kbar. This is high in the context of other reported spin-crossover barocalorics, and competitive within the field at large. The excellent performance results from a large barocaloric coefficient (dT1/2/dp = 35K kbar−1). In addition, the one-pot synthesis is simple and free from toxic solvents.
items.authors: Matthew G. Robb, Anthony E. Phillips, Lukas Sippach, Andreas Rydh, Gregor Kieslich, Hanna L B Boström

items.title: Water-Responsive Shape-Memory Origami Enabled by a Washi–Bulk pNIPAAm Hydrogel Hybrid Sheet
items.abstract: Origami transforms two-dimensional sheets into complex three-dimensional forms through folding and has evolved from a traditional art into a versatile design principle for deployable and reconfigurable structures. Here, we develop a water-responsive shape-memory origami sheet by combining highly concentrated poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (bulk pNIPAAm) hydrogel with Japanese kozo paper. Bulk pNIPAAm undergoes pronounced hydrationinduced softening and recovers its permanent shape upon rehydration, whereas the paper scaffold enables the hydrogel to be fabricated and handled as a thin, foldable sheet. Rather than programming only individual active creases, the hybrid sheet allows complex folded three-dimensional configurations to be programmed directly as permanent shapes. Two complementary programming strategies are demonstrated: photopolymerization of precursorimpregnated paper in a pre-folded configuration and post-fabrication programming by local photopolymerization at selected creases. Kozo washi-based hybrid sheets exhibited more than 90% recovery within several seconds in a simple folding test, and Miura-fold, crane, dolphin, and kirigami structures recovered their memorized geometries after unfolding and dehydration-induced temporary fixation. Finally, simply pouring warm water onto a flowershaped structure triggers spontaneous blooming without full immersion. This approach transforms a bulk shape-memory hydrogel into a fold-programmable sheet material and
items.authors: Kohei Murata, Hiroaki Suzuki

items.title: Kinetically Synchronized Aqueous Co-precipitation and Hydrothermal Crystallisation of (Mg1−xCox)CO3 Rhombohedral Solid-Solution Nanoparticles: Thermodynamic Feasibility, Ethylene Glycol Kinetic Control, and Prospective Functional Applications
items.abstract: Cobaltoan magnesite, (Mg1−xCox)CO3 (R3c; x = 0–1), has previously been accessible only under extreme solid-state conditions (≥600 °C, ≥15 kbar; Goldsmith Northrop, 1965) or over geological timescales in supergene ore environments (Barton et al., 2014). We report the first deliberate laboratory synthesis of phase-pure (Mg,Co)CO3 solid-solution nanoparticles at 250 °C under autogenous pressure (~40 bar) via a modified polyol-assisted aqueous coprecipitation route. Thermodynamic feasibility is established through saturation-index analysis (SI(CoCO3) = +10.6, ΔG° = −60.5 kJ mol−1; SI(MgCO3) = +2.6, ΔG° = −14.8 kJ mol−1), confirming that both carbonate end-members are thermodynamically driven to precipitate from solution at ambient conditions and that the hydrothermal step supplies kinetic — not thermodynamic — activation energy. The principal kinetic challenge, the seven-order-ofmagnitude disparity in solubility products (Ksp(CoCO3) = 10−13 vs. 6.8×10−6 for MgCO3), is surmounted by ethylene glycol (EG) coordination of Co2+, confirmed in situ by a spontaneous pink→blue colour transition upon EG addition, which elevates the desolvation activation barrier and synchronises Co2+ and Mg2+ precipitation rates. Convergent evidence from five independent characterisation techniques confirms the R3c solid-solution product: (i) PXRD with Vegard's Law analysis of the composition-sensitive (113) reflection yields x(Co) ≈ 0.73 (Sample 3, pre-hydrothermal) and x(Co) ≈ 0.44 (Sample 4, post-hydrothermal); (ii) FTIR reveals a single ν2(CO32−) band at 870 cm−1, intermediate between MgCO3 (880) and CoCO3 (860 cm−1) endmembers — a necessary and sufficient criterion for isomorphic solid-solution identification by infrared spectroscopy; (iii) SEM-EDX shows a continuous unimodal composition distribution (x(Co) = 0.27–0.73) with no bimodal clustering indicative of phase separation; (iv) UV–Vis spectroscopy identifies characteristic Co2+ ligand-field and charge-transfer transitions with a direct optical band gap of ~3.1–3.4 eV; (v) DLS confirms near-monodisperse product (PDI = 0.053, Dh = 306 nm) following hydrothermal treatment, representing an 83% reduction in polydispersity relative to the amorphous precursor (PDI = 0.314). Prospective applications spanning heterogeneous catalysis, Li-ion battery cathode precursors, CO2 mineralisation, photocatalysis, and pH-responsive drug delivery are evaluated on the basis of the crystal chemistry and mixed-metal composition of the product phase.
items.authors: Abdul Haseeb Tanoli, Arfeen, Laiba Irshad Khattak, Tasbiha Rehman Bhatti, Muhammad Muneeb Yousafzai, Tayyaba Ghani

items.title: Electrochemical Detection of Ethanol in Liquid Samples and Simulated Breath: Investigating Calibration, Selectivity, and Preconcentration
items.abstract: Advances in miniaturized and point-of-care electrochemical sensors have expanded their applications in healthcare, environmental monitoring, and public safety. Consequently, it is important to study the principles of these technologies in an undergraduate setting. This experiment uses screen-printed electrodes for electrochemical detection of ethanol and introduces students to electrocatalysis, calibration curves, chemical interference, selectivity, and preconcentration. Students use cyclic voltammetry and chronoamperometry to make calibration curves and determine ethanol concentrations in ethanol standards and diluted beer and wine samples.
